Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house appreciates the report which the minister has just made, as I am sure all hon. members here and indeed all Canadians appreciate the fact that the Secretary of State of the United States was able to stop off in Ottawa on his way back to Geneva.
I should like to associate myself and our party with what the minister has said about the new Secretary of State. I am sure all Canadians wish him well on the occasion of this conference and on future occasions of this kind. I am sure we all agree with the minister when he said that Mr. Herter is

Motions for Papers
peculiarly qualified by experience and by ability to carry on the important work that has been entrusted to him. It is well that the Canadian government should be informed on these matters even though we may not be represented at the particular meeting, because our commitments and our responsibilities are definitely and deeply involved. If there is to be that essential unity inside the coalition that we all work for there must be this kind of consultation in advance of decision.
I quite appreciate the fact that it would be unfair to ask the minister to give us details of the negotiations which are taking place. That is not the way in which negotiations can best be conducted. But I think we are agreed that the principle which underlies these negotiations should be the maintenance of western rights in Berlin and that if there is to be any alteration of the situation there, it should not be at the expense of those rights. I think Mr. Herter's visit also emphasizes the unity inside the western coalition, which as I said is essential and is perhaps one of the most gratifying features of the earlier negotiations. Although there have been disappointments in the past I hope that during the weeks ahead, if there are to be further meetings, with this strong, fundamental unity among the three western foreign ministers, and with flexibility in negotiation, perhaps the new session will be able to come to some satisfactory conclusion.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL GRANTS TO NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the payment of additional grants to the province of Newfoundland.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. McCleave in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL GRANTS TO NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
The resolution
before the committee asks leave to introduce a measure to provide for the payment of additional grants to the province of Newfoundland. The bill for the introduction of which leave is now sought will provide authority for the payment to the province of Newfoundland of amounts recommended by the royal commission on the terms of union with Newfoundland for the fiscal years 195758 to 1961-62 inclusive. This bill may well find itself placed among the important constitutional documents of our country. The operative portion of the measure is brief but the bill will contain extensive recitals. Having regard to the nature and importance of this legislation I may say I hope to approach the subject in keeping with the seriousness of it for the Canadian confederation.
Ten years have passed, sir, since Newfoundland, the Atlantic outpost of this continent, joined the Canadian family. This act of confederation brought a sense of completion to the farsighted work of the fathers of confederation which had not been until that time, attained. The only regret of Canadians in the other parts of Canada was that Newfoundland's entry into the Canadian family had been long delayed. Had Newfoundland come in during earlier years Newfoundlanders and other Canadians, in this expanded realm, might have grown together and Newfoundlanders might have played their influential part from the beginning of confederation in fashioning the history of this new young nation and adding to her glories and her destiny, as they are doing now and as Newfoundlanders will continue to do.
Forty-four years had passed since the last provincial members had been previously added to confederation, in 1905, and all Canadians welcomed with enthusiasm the entry of Newfoundland into the Canadian family. This is the spirit, I am sure, in which the house approaches this present measure today. It is in the larger spirit of the larger Canada.
Our concern in this present measure must, of course, relate to the financial basis of

Grants to Newfoundland Newfoundland's confederation with Canada.
I shall not delay the committee by any extended review of the financial terms of confederation. They are contained in articles 23 to 29 of the terms of confederation.
Article 23 related to the assumption of debt. Article 24 related to the disposal of the financial surplus that Newfoundland had at that time; article 25 to the retention by Newfoundland of its interest in the proceeds of a particular loan at that time. Article 26 provided for the payment of annual subsidies by Canada to the province of Newfoundland, and it is under that provision that the subsidies have been paid in the interval. Article 27 provided for the entry of Newfoundland into a tax agreement with Canada similar to that which had been entered into by the majority of the provinces at that time in relation to the sharing of the proceeds of the direct standard taxes. Article 28 provided for the payment of a series of annual transitional grants over a period of 12 years by Canada to Newfoundland.
These grants, for the first three years, were to be in the amount of $6,500,000 each, and from that point they graduated down until in the tenth year the amount was to be $1,050,000; in the eleventh year, $700,000, and in the twelfth year, $350,000. The last of these payments will be made in the fiscal year which will end on March 31, 1961.
Then we proceed to article 29, from which the measure now under discussion stems. The background of article 29 of the terms of union is, I am sure, well known to all members of the house. There existed at the time of confederation wide differences in the degree of development attained in Newfoundland as compared with the rest of Canada. Newfoundland, with Labrador, is a land of vast resources, but while there had been some development of those resources the great period of their development lay in the future. There was in Newfoundland a pronounced lack of what has come to be known as social capital, public investment in roads, schools, hospitals and other services. Communication was limited. The island government, however, was virtually free of debt.
Under these circumstances it was quite clear to those who negotiated the terms of confederation that following the union there would be what I might call a period of bridging the gaps. Premier Smallwood has called it a period of transition. The gaps which it was contemplated would need to be bridged involved time, first, to equalize services in Newfoundland wih those in other parts of Canada, and time also, in the second place, to develop the tremendous potential of Newfoundland. So far as the equalization of

services was concerned, regard was had in term 29 to the state of taxation in the three maritime provinces.
I have stressed that this was a period of bridging the gaps or, as Mr. Smallwood has called it, a period of transition. It was not contemplated that this period would last forever. On the contrary, it was thought of as a period that would be limited in time, but at that stage no one could say how long the period would continue.
Now, sir, I think it appropriate to examine the terms of article 29. It reads as follows:
In view of the difficulty of predicting with sufficient accuracy the financial consequences to Newfoundland of becoming a province of Canada, the government of Canada will appoint a royal commission within eight years from the date of union to review the financial position of the province of Newfoundland and to recommend the form and scale of additional financial assistance, if any, that may be required by the government of the province of Newfoundland to enable it to continue public services at the levels and standards reached subsequent to the date of union, without resorting to taxation more burdensome, having regard to capacity to pay, than that obtaining generally in the region comprising the maritime provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island.
It may be, Mr. Chairman, that the terms of this article have not been always clearly understood. It may be that in a sense they have been oversold in the understanding of some in relation to the fair interpretation of this important article. It is clear on examination that the elements in this article of union are as follows. First, the royal commission was to be a federal royal commission. In the second place, it was to be appointed within a period of eight years after the first day of April, 1949. No time was set for the completion of the hearings of the royal commission or the date of its report. The provision simply was that the appointment should be made before March 31, 1957. The reason given in the article for the appointment of the royal commission is in the opening words. It relates to the difficulty of predicting with sufficient accuracy the financial consequences to Newfoundland of becoming a province of Canada.
The purpose the royal commission was to serve was twofold. First, it was to conduct a review and, second, it was to make recommendations. It was in the first place to review the financial position of the province of Newfoundland, and in the second place it was to recommend the form and scale of additional financial assistance, if any, that might be required by Newfoundland. "Additional financial assistance" obviously means in addition to the transitional grants provided for in article 28 and the subsidies provided in article 26. The purpose of the additional

financial assistance, if any, was, first, to continue the public services reached in the postunion period. It is quite clear, and this has been a matter of comment since, that it was not to improve these services but to continue them. And second, this was to be done without resorting to taxation heavier in relation to capacity to pay than obtained in the three maritime provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.
The terms of reference of the royal commission were thus completely defined in article 29. The article, it may seem strange to some in reading it, makes no provision whatever for what is to follow the report of the royal commission. It is completely silent on that point. It gives no indication of what disposal shall be made of the recommendations the royal commission might make. Indeed, in terms of the express obligations created by this article it is quite clear that the only obligation expressly created on the part of the federal government was the appointment of a royal commission.
This limited extent of the provisions of article 29 was clearly recognized in the debate in this house on the terms of union, which occurred in February, 1949. The then prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, in introducing the resolution on February 7, 1949 made this comment on article 29 as recorded at page 289 of Hansard:
It was also provided that within eight years from the coming into force of the terms of union a commission would be set up to examine the situation anew, and to report as to whether or not the terms provided are working satisfactorily and are sufficient to bring about the object of equalizing the lot of the people of the new province with that of the people of the older provinces. There is no undertaking to implement any terms of recommendation that may be made at that time by a royal commission. It was felt by the Newfoundland delegation, and by the representatives of the Canadian government, that this was something that was being entered into in a spirit of fairness on both sides, and that it was not necessary to make binding stipulations about what would happen with respect to the report of a royal commission. It was felt if there was an investigation and a report b.y a commission, in which the public at that time would have confidence, the legislators of that day could well be trusted to do what would prove to be right in order to make this enlarged nation a united nation continuing on its path of progress toward its great destiny.
I am sure every hon. member of this present parliament would applaud in full that comment made by Mr. St. Laurent on February 7, 1949. It is unquestionably an interpretation of the terms of article 29 to which no exception can be taken by anyone and it correctly expresses, I am sure, the spirit of the Canadian parliament in this day and in the days to come.
Grants to Newfoundland I may say that the same issue arose in the hearings of the royal commission, as was indeed inevitable. I will just mention several of the passages in the proceedings of the royal commission where the question arose. At page 1504 of the proceedings the chairman of the royal commission, Chief Justice McNair of New Brunswick, made this comment on the terms of article 29 and the work of the royal commission. He said:
Anything we do here will have no binding effect. Further, at pages 1512 and 1513 the chairman said, and this time his remarks were replied to by Mr. Carl Goldenberg, the very distinguished counsel who represented the province of Newfoundland before the royal commission:
A number of questions arise in my mind on this point, Mr. Goldenberg. Our recommendation alone-
That is the recommendation of the commission.
-will create nothing binding.
Mr. Goldenberg replied "No". Then the chairman commented further on page 1513: Our recommendation alone has no effect.
To this Mr. Goldenberg replied:
It is only a recommendation to the government of Canada.
Premier Smallwood, and I add this for the completion of the record on this subject, at pages 1604 and 1605 apparently approached the question from a slightly different point of view. In speaking of term 29 he said:
-but spells out-I thought until this hearing- very carefully and very clearly the actual words of the terms of reference.
He proceeded to base his argument on the terms and he said:
The recommendations you make-
He was addressing the royal commission. -will morally bind not only the government of Canada to submit them to the parliament of Canada with their own qualified recommendation, but will morally bind the parliament of Canada to adopt them.
Premier Smallwood was there basing his argument on a moral obligation, while it was quite clear it was the stated view of the commission, as it was of the eminent counsel who appeared on behalf of Newfoundland before the royal commission, that there was no explicit or binding obligation. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I pause at this time simply to draw this inference in the light of the statements of Mr. St. Laurent, who was prime minister in 1949, and the statements by Chief Justice McNair and Mr. Goldenberg that what we do now in this parliament in 1959 is not done under any literal compulsion or binding stipulation, for there is none in article 29 or

Grants to Newfoundland elsewhere. What we do now is an expression of the desire of the Canadian parliament and the Canadian people to be just and fair to our new partner in confederation, according to the abiding conceptions of justice and fair play of the Canadian people and their parliament.
These are the same conceptions of justice and fair play which animated the Canadians in 1867, in 1870, in 1871, in 1873 and in 1905 on the occasion of the accession of the other provinces to the federated family. It is the same spirit in which I am sure we can trust the parliament of Canada in the year 1962 to approach the same problem.
The royal commission was appointed by the former government on February 21, 1957 in fulfilment and discharge of the obligation created by article 29. The order in council naturally follows precisely and verbatim the language of article 29. I think regard must be had naturally to the personnel of the royal commission, particularly in the light of the language used by Mr. St. Laurent as I quoted him in 1949 when he referred to the commission at that time as men in whom the public would have confidence. Three distinguished commissioners were chosen; one was the chief justice of New Brunswick, Chief Justice McNair, who was chairman of the commission; the next member of the commission was Sir Albert Walsh, chief justice of Newfoundland, who had participated as one of the representatives of Newfoundland in the negotiation of the terms of union. The third member was Mr. John Deutsch, former assistant deputy minister of finance.
I do not need to say, I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that any royal commission composed of men of the experience and capacity of the members of this commission must be regarded with great respect in any part of Canada. The personnel of this commission was quite evidently chosen by the Canadian government of that time in consultation with the government of Newfoundland, because it is quite clear that the personnel of the commission was completely satisfactory to the government of Newfoundland. I have before me a press dispatch dated February 25, 1957, which appeared in the Charlottetown Guardian and which reads:
A beaming Premier Smallwood groped for superlatives Friday to express his delight at the choice of members for the royal commission to review Newfoundland's financial terms of union with Canada.
Work of the commission, whose appointment was announced in the commons Friday by Prime Minister St. Laurent, would be "of absolutely terrific importance to Newfoundland," Mr. Smallwood told a press conference.
The future of Newfoundland's "standards and levels of services will be determined by the recommendations of the commission," he said. It would recommend "the form and scale" of additional financial assistance.

Commission chairman John McNair, chief justice and former premier of New Brunswick, was "long a personal friend of mine," Mr. Smallwood said. Mr. McNair was "a famous fighter for maritime rights and after we went in for Atlantic provinces rights."
John James Deutsch was "probably the most knowledgeable man in all Canada of federal-provincial affairs." He was "a great friend of Newfoundland ... a man of great sympathy for Newfoundland."
Of Newfoundland Chief Justice Sir Albert Walsh, third of the three commission members, Mr. Smallwood said "Newfoundland could be searched from end to end and we would not find a better man to represent Newfoundland on this royal commission. He is thoroughly informed."
When we as a government came into office on June 21, 1957 the royal commission had not yet commenced its sittings, and asked for directions from the new government in that respect. We requested the royal commission to carry on, and did everything in our power as a government to facilitate their inquiry.
The royal commission had not proceeded very far before it encountered the inevitable difficulties raised by the vague and nebulous terms of the reference which had been taken from article 29. The difficulties confronting the royal commission revolved principally around the problem of projecting a selected year into the indefinite future. It was the difficulty of determining future needs on the basis of past conditions.
This problem is quite clear to anyone reading the report, and it confronted the royal commission with constant difficulties. I shall not detain the committee by an extended review or an attempt at an extended review of the report of the royal commission. I am assuming that all hon. members are acquainted with its contents. Perhaps I might just mention a few passages in passing to emphasize the highlights of the report, both as to the difficulties confronting the royal commission and as to their findings. On page 3 we find this sentence:
The economy of Newfoundland was more highly dependent upon external markets than any Canadian region.
On page 4:
The new provincial government came into existence virtually free of debt and with $40 million in its treasury. These substantial resources were available for the improvement of public services and the promotion of economic development. However, these tasks had to be assumed under a number of serious handicaps. Unlike the rest of Canada, Newfoundland had not received the benefits of over 80 years of aggressive federal policies designed to assist economic development and to foster economic expansion. Newfoundland had been outside the great national structure of transportation facilities, highly developed government services, and extensive regional and industrial supports. Newfoundland was without a modern system of transportation. In the greater part of the populated area there were no roads whatever and in

the remainder only a few miles were up to modern standards. The natural resources were largely unsurveyed and unexplored. Very few intensive investigations had been carried out. Little or no research had been applied to problems of untiliza-tion and marketing, even in the fisheries.
At page 5:
In this respect Newfoundland was at about the same stage as the maritime provinces were in 1867.
At page 8-

Yes, I shall be glad to read them. I am trying to pick out the essential highlights of the report without spending too much time on it. The words in the interval between those two last passages are as follows:
"Newfoundland has had a long history of poverty: and this poverty meant the neglect of the public services."
That quotation is taken from the submis-mission of the province of Newfoundland to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects. The report continues:
The deficiency in the public services was strongly evident in the lack of social capital and in the limited development of the social services. Aside from St. John's, and a few other centres the province was without municipal organizations or municipal facilities. In this respect Newfoundland was at about the same stage as the maritime provinces were in 1867.
At page 8:
There have been few really major improvements in the levels and standards of services. The deficiencies of the past have not been substantially overcome.
Further down:
The Newfoundland portion of the trans-Canada highway is not more than a quarter completed in terms of total estimated cost. There is no transprovincial road whatever. The majority of the numerous small settlements in the province are still without any road connections.
Further down:
In short, Newfoundland is confronted with the urgent task of modernization, but is without the modern means of mobility and communication.
At the bottom of the page and extending over to page 9:
The average per capita incomes in Newfoundland are further affected by the more limited opportunities for female workers and by the fact that the proportion of the population of working age is significantly smaller than elsewhere in Canada. In 1956, 41 per cent of the population of Newfoundland was under 15 years of age as compared with 32 per cent for Canada as a whole.
Further down on page 9:
The addition of Labrador to Canadian territory has added also another frontier rich in minerals and water power. Labrador is already making
Grants to Newfoundland its contribution to the vital role which undeveloped frontiers have played in the history of national economic expansion.
Then on page 16 in the course of the financial review the report proceeds:
The total of the federal payments-
This is in the post-union period.
-comprised 73 per cent of the total provincial net revenue in the fiscal year ending March 31, 1951 and 48 per cent in the fiscal year ending March 31, 1957.
Further down on the same page:
In other words, during the past three years the revenues of the province on ordinary account have fallen more and more short of the requirements for ordinary expenditures.
Further down on the same page:
In the most recent fiscal year ending March 31, 1958, the estimated financial requirement was nearly $16 million, all of which would have had to be borrowed.
Then on page 18:
In the early years the debt position of the provincial government was very favourable. At the outset the provincial government had in hand a substantial net cash surplus and was virtually free of any net debt charges. Since 1952 the provincial debt has increased steadily.
And further down:
The total estimated net direct and indirect debt of the government of Newfoundland outstanding on March 31, 1958, was $71.0 million. This total amounted to $163 per capita compared with about twice this amount per capita for the governments of the maritime provinces combined. These comparisons would appear to indicate that the debt position of the government of Newfoundland continues to be favourable in relation to the maritime provinces.
Then on page 19 the commission enters upon chapter III which relates to the levels and standards of public services in Newfoundland. Here on page 19 the report points out-

I thank the committee, Mr. Chairman. On page 19 the report states as follows:
It must be assumed that the phrase "the levels and standards reached subsequent to the date of union" means the highest levels and standards reached. Otherwise term 29 has little meaning.
And further down:
The brief presented on behalf of the government of the province of Newfoundland in support of additional financial assistance assumes that the highest levels and standards of public service reached subsequent to the date of union were reached in the fiscal year 1956-57.
Then at page 25:
The calculations show that there has been a fairly steady improvement in the per capita levels

Grants to Newfoundland
and standards of public service over the period 1949 to 1956 although half of that improvement was due to increased federal grants in aid. The level of service in 1956 was about 22 per cent higher than in 1949.
Then, Mr. Chairman, I turn to page 37, where the commission concludes its chapter on the burden of taxation with this observation:
-we have come to the conclusion that the burdens imposed by the present tax systems of Newfoundland and the maritime provinces are of the same order and that, for the purposes of our inquiry, we should regard the burden as approximately equal.
Then at page 38 begins the important and final chapter V containing the recommendations of the commission. At page 38, after setting out certain tables, the commission reaches the conclusion that the revenue deficiency-and this is the final line of the table-including the transitional grant of $2,250,000 is $5,190,000 for the fiscal year in 1956-57. The commission's observation on this table is as follows:
It will be seen from the above table that the total requirements for 1956-57 exceeded the total revenue, exclusive of the transitional grant, by $5,190,000. In other words, on the basis of 1956-57 the province would require additional revenue of $5,190,000 less the transitional grant of $2,250,000, or $2,940,000, to continue public services at the levels and standards reached.
Then at page 39 in the next paragraph following we find this:
The terms of reference require the determination of the additional financial assistance necessary to continue public services at the levels and standards reached subsequent to union. In our view the words "to continue" involve consideration of the future at least as far as to make some assessment of the probable course of revenues and expenditures. While it is impossible to project the expenditure requirements and revenues of the province into the future, we feel that we should give consideration to the financial position of the provincial government as indicated by the estimates for the year 1957-58 furnished to us by the financial adviser to the province.
Then the commission proceeds to set forth a table relating to the fiscal year 1957-58, which concludes with this line:
Estimated revenue deficiency, including the transitional grant of $1,400,000, $8,102,000.
On that point the commission makes this comment:
The revenue deficiency indicated by the above table amounts to an estimated $8,102,000 inclusive of the transitional grant of $1,400,000 or $6,702,000 excluding the transitional grant.
Then on page 40, the final page of the report, the commission, after saying that with respect to the year 1957-58 the recession is no more than a temporary condition, proceeds to this final paragraph of the report:
After giving consideration to the deficiency in revenue indicated by our calculations for the fiscal

years 1956-57 and 1958-59 and after attempting to make a fair and equitable assessment in respect of the uncertainties and special factors mentioned above, we find that the government of Newfoundland requires, as from April, 1957, additional financial assistance of $8,000,000 per annum, less the transitional grant while it applies, "to enable it to continue public services at the levels and standards reached subsequent to the date of union without resorting to taxation more burdensome, having regard to capacity to pay, than that obtaining generally in the region comprising the maritime provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island". Accordingly we recommend additional financial assistance as follows:
(a)	for the fiscal year beginning April 1, 1957, $8,000,00 less the transitional grant of $1,400,000 or, $6,600,000;
(b)	for the fiscal year beginning April 1, 1958, $8,000,000 less the transitional grant of $1,050,000 or, $6,950,000;
(c)	for the fiscal year beginning April 1, 1959, $8,000,000 less the transitional grant of $700,000 or, $7,300,000;
(d)	for the fiscal year beginning April 1, 1960, $8,000,000 less the transitional grant of $350,000 or $7,650,000;
(e)	thereafter $8,000,000 per annum.
The report concludes at that point. It is signed by the three commissioners and evidently is a unanimous report. I have already said, Mr. Chairman, that having regard to the personnel of this royal commission its recommendations are entitled to great respect.
There are two questions which arise, I think, when anyone reads this report. The first is as to why, without any explanation, in the final chapter the royal commission departed from the year 1956-57, which was the basic year upon which all the evidence had been submitted up to that point, and chose to base its recommendation on the fiscal year 1957-58. That question remains unanswered.
The second question which arises is as to what the commission meant by the word "thereafter" in the final line of the final recommendation. This naturally presents a question, and in endeavouring to determine the meaning to be given to this expression in the report one must of course have regard to the fact that these commissioners are not men who are given to expressing themselves in words of imprecise meaning. Had they meant to say that these payments were to run indefinitely I think it might be expected that they would have said so explicitly. Certain it is that the province of Newfoundland did not ask or expect the royal commission to make any recommendations of this nature that would have indefinite effect. Indeed, counsel for the province, Mr. Golden-berg, in his submission dealt with this subject explicitly. At page 621 of the proceedings

Mr. Goldenberg, after dealing with the annual amount sought by the province of Newfoundland, made this comment:
This is the minimum additional financial assistance now required in order to continue the existing levels and standards oi services on a most conservative basis. It is not suggested, however, that such assistance will be required indefinitely.
Then further, at pages 627 and 628, Mr. Goldenberg, the eminent counsel for Newfoundland, again dealt with this aspect in his submission to the royal commission on July 26. He said:
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am not suggesting that this additional financial assistance will be required by Newfoundland indefinitely. As Newfoundland's public services improve and its economy expands, the differentials in income and in tax burdens as compared with other provinces will narrow; with the narrowing of the gap, the dependence on grants from the government of Canada will decline. Accordingly, while Newfoundland is now entitled, under the provisions of term 29 of the terms of union, to receive additional annual financial assistance of the order of $17,000,000, provision should be made for a further review of its financial and economic position within a reasonable period of time.
Accordingly, Mr. Chairman, on behalf of the government of Newfoundland I submit that the government of Newfoundland is entitled to claim from the government of Canada an annual grant of $17,000,000 subject to the adjustments which we have discussed over and above all other federal grants as the additional financial assistance required under the explicit provisions of term 29. I recommend further that the said grant should be paid annually to the province of Newfoundland, commencing in the fiscal year 1957-58. I recommend that the amount of the said annual grant should thereafter be subject to periodic review. That, Mr. Chairman, completes my presentation of the case under term 29.
I may add, Mr. Chairman, that throughout the hearings on more than one occasion the same theme had been reiterated, that the annual amounts which were being asked for by Newfoundland were not being asked on the basis of a period of indefinite duration but that there should be a further and later review.
Mr. Chairman, I do not need to remind the house of the reaction of the government of Newfoundland to the report when it was made public in July of 1958. If I say the report was received with keen disappointment in Newfoundland, I perhaps understate the reaction in the tenth province. This subject was discussed in this house last September, and I am sure I do not need to remind hon. members of the expressions used on that occasion. However, the discussion occurred, on September 4 and 6 and the comments of the premier of Newfoundland on the recommendations are recorded in Hansard at page 4724 of September 6. Feelings in Newfoundland were obviously deeply disturbed by the
Grants to Newfoundland report, and the comments of the head of the government of the province were put in strong terms.
A meeting followed, Mr. Chairman, in Ottawa last January 26. Premier Smallwood and Mr. Spencer, the provincial treasurer of Newfoundland, came to Ottawa accompanied by Mr. A. B. Perlin, who had been a member of the royal commission which had prepared the submission which the province made to the federal royal commission, as well as Mr. Carl Goldenberg, the counsel. Premier Smallwood and Mr. Spencer met with the Prime Minister and myself in the morning. The conference continued in the afternoon without the Prime Minister, but officials of the Department of Finance were also present on this occasion.
I am not going to review in detail the nature of the extended and friendly discussions which were held at that time. Premier Smallwood was highly critical of the report of the royal commission. He criticized it on various grounds, and he asked that the federal government provide larger payments than those recommended. He pressed for a review at a later date on the subject of fiscal relations between the province and the dominion. He pointed out he had previously recommended that there should be this further and later review. In the course of the discussion possible dates for such a review were mentioned, and Mr. Smallwood suggested that in view of the imponderables in the situation concerning the future, this review should take place in the year 1965, or thereabouts; and he referred to the fact, as he put it, that there had already been ten reviews of the financial provision made on behalf of the maritime provinces in confederation since 1867.
I turn now to recall to the minds of hon. members that in the meantime, since the royal commission had been appointed in the spring of 1957, this government had moved, I think I may say swiftly, to enlarge the payments made to Newfoundland which were not related to the provisions of term 29. The Atlantic provinces adjustment grants came into effect on April 1, 1958, and provided for payments out of the federal treasury to the four Atlantic provinces of a total of $100 million over the four fiscal years then commencing. That provision had followed approval given to it at the dominion-provincial conference in November, 1957, and a meeting of representatives of the governments of the four Atlantic provinces at Halifax later in 1957, at which agreement had been reached as to the distribution of this $25 million annual payment from the federal treasury.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL GRANTS TO NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
I hope not to detain the committee much longer. The government was faced with the necessity of making a decision with respect to the recommendations contained in the report of the _ royal commission, and to make such a decision in the light of what I have said about the extent of the provisions of article 29, of what I have said about the importance to be attached to the recommendation of the royal commission, the reservations on certain aspects, which one has on reading the report, and also the objections taken to the recommendation by the premier of Newfoundland notwithstanding what was said earlier about the personnel of the royal commission.
Under all the circumstances the government has decided to ask this house to make the following provision by the present bill. It has been decided to ask the house to provide for payments by the federal treasury to Newfoundland for the five-year period commencing April 1, 1957, and concluding March 31, 1962, at the rates recommended by the royal commission. The five-year period in question coincides with the current five-year period of agreements entered into in pursuance of the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act. Indeed, it coincides with the current five-year period prescribed by that particular enactment of this parliament.
If the bill receives the approval of parliament there will be provision made for payment in respect of these five years of course, over and above the transitional grants which expire on March 31, 1961, of a total of $36,500,000. Of this sum nearly one-half will become payable forthwith. The payments that were recommended for the fiscal years 1957-58 and 1958-59 and the first of the two semi-annual payments for the current fiscal year, 1959-60, will become immediately due and payable, and they aggregate $17.2 million.
It is proposed that this provision be made on a continuing basis by this bill, and that the matter should not be left to be dealt with by items in the annual estimates. In this respect the bill gives effect to the request made by Premier Smallwood. The payments, of course, will be unconditional.
The second aspect of the matter concerns what is to follow March 31, 1962. Already, as a result of decisions taken at the dominion-provincial conference of finance ministers and provincial treasurers last Monday and Tuesday, a comprehensive study of all aspects of federal-provincial fiscal relations has been proposed, approved and launched.
I point out that this bill notes and states that in the course of that comprehensive review not only will the circumstances of Newfoundland be taken into account along with

those, of course, of any other provinces, but that any special circumstances relating to Newfoundland will be taken into account in determining the financial relations between Canada and Newfoundland after March 31, 1962. This position is clearly set out in a recital in the bill. Thus parliament is invited to place itself on record as giving to Newfoundland an assurance which, we are led to understand, means much to Newfoundland and to which that province will, it is expected, attach no little importance.
This, then, is the approach of the government in this important matter, and I think it may be quite fair to say that it is an approach in the spirit of confederation that we believe will be served through the medium of this significant measure. In conclusion may I point out that all financial relations between the dominion and the ten provinces of this country must be reviewed as at April 1, 1962.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, would the minister permit a question at this point. He said "must be reviewed". Could the minister give the statutory authority for that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL GRANTS TO NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
1 am not referring to statutory authority, Mr. Chairman. If my hon. friend will allow me to proceed I think he will see quite clearly what I mean. I point out that every province is concerned in what happens as from April 1, 1962, in regard to the financial relations between the dominion and the provinces. It is with this fact in mind that we proposed the comprehensive study which was approved and inaugurated last week. It is quite clear that Newfoundland's fiscal relations with the dominion are explicitly included in the scope of this comprehensive study. That is the setting in which this review will occur, as the Prime Minister said in this house in his statement of March 25.
What may be said of special claims on the part of Newfoundland? It is quite clear in the light of the difficulties the royal commissioners had to face that it would be impossible to make calculations today on that subject. No one can project that far in the future in a period when the development of resources in Newfoundland and Labrador is proceeding at a very rapid pace, and when the population is increasing at an unprecedented rate, and when many other changes are taking place. Therefore the bill expressly states in one of the recitals that "any special circumstances relating to the financial position of the province of Newfoundland after March 31, 1962, would be taken into consideration".
We have sought in this measure to spell out this matter in parliamentary form, indeed in

black and white. May I remind hon. members that apart from the constitutional subsidies, no other province-not one of the other nine provinces-has anything in black and white beyond March 31, 1962, to define its financial relations with the dominion; yet does anyone doubt that honourable solutions of fiscal problems between the provinces and the dominion after that date will be earnestly sought? This is the way the Canadian confederation has worked, and in the view of the government this is the way the Canadian confederation will work in 1962 and in years to come.
As a government we have endeavoured to demonstrate our concern over the fiscal problems confronting the provinces and the municipalities. We have enlarged our own federal burdens in order to assist the provinces and municipalities to meet theirs. As I have already endeavoured to point out, there is no binding stipulation on the federal government under article 29 to follow in any way the terms of any recommendations made by the royal commission; yet in the same spirit that animated Mr. St. Laurent in his statement in the house in February, 1949, which I read earlier, we are asking the house to appropriate by this bill for the period ending March 31, 1962, the sum of $36,500,000. In this way we are inviting parliament to express the desire of parliament and the Canadian people to be just and fair to Newfoundland.
Likewise there was no obligation on parliament to make any such provision as is now made through the medium of the Atlantic provinces adjustment grant; yet parliament made that provision and the four Atlantic provinces are deriving the benefits thereof today. Why was that done? While there was no legal obligation to do it, it was an expression on the part of the Canadian parliament of its view that the Canadian people are one family and that we must have regard to the problems of all sections of this great country. That measure was an expression of the spirit of confederation. It was an expression of the concern of the dominion, with the concurrence of the other six provinces, at the conference of November, 1957, over the well-being of the four provinces down by the sea. That concern, Mr. Chairman, will continue.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL GRANTS TO NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the committee will have listened, I know, with the greatest possible interest to the statement the minister has just made on the resolution before us. If I may quote the words of the minister as I took them down, "having regard to the importance and the nature" of the subject matter of this resolution, dealing as it does with fundamental matters concerning our confederation, it seems to me that it would have been more appropriate to have had this legislation introduced and sponsored in the house by the Prime Minister, the leader of the government. I say that without, of course, any disrespect to the minister who has put the case as he sees it before us this morning very clearly and in very moderate terms and tones. But I think it would have been even more appropriate if the Prime Minister had taken the responsibility for this legislation because of the statement he made on this matter in March last, and I will have something to say about that later.
This resolution deals with a matter which in a sense is concerned with the completion of the work of confederation. There was no

Grants to Newfoundland single move made by the previous government, of which I had the honour to be a member for some years, which caused our party greater pride than that which brought about, except in regard to this one bit of unfinished business, the completion of this great work of unity in confederation, this great work of national development which had eluded the efforts of Canadian and Newfoundland statesmen for many, many years before it was successfully accomplished ten years ago.
There was, however, as I have said, one piece of unfinished financial business which was in a sense postponed but is dealt with in an article which is an integral part of the terms of union, article 29. Term 29, as it is called, was as much a condition of union as any other article of this fundamental pact which brought about union. We should keep it very much in our minds that if term 29 had not been included perhaps confederation could not have been completed at that time. I think those of us who had something to do with the negotiations which were so successfully concluded then will all agree as to the importance of term 29.
That article, just as much as the others, constituted a specific and solemn undertaking given by the Canadian government and accepted as satisfactory by the government of Newfoundland as the result of which two sovereign nations-I admit that one of them at that time had its sovereignty temporarily in a commission-within the commonwealth of nations signed a pact, a treaty if you like, which provided for their union. Indeed in that sense, because of the circumstances that surrounded the negotiations at that time ten years ago, the negotiations and this pact, if you want to call it that, differed from the negotiations, agreements and arrangements which covered the colonies coming into a confederation through an act of the British parliament in the nineteenth century. That is the way term 29 as part of the pact of union is regarded by the people of Newfoundland, and I think it is the way it should be regarded by all Canadians.
Perhaps I might put on the record, because I think it correctly reflects the views of the people of Newfoundland with regard to the significance of term 29, an excerpt from the budget speech of the minister of finance of Newfoundland, Hon. Mr. Spencer, on June 26 of this year. I quote what he had to say at that time in the Newfoundland legislature:
It will be useful, I think, if I put the simple facts on the record. These facts are unmistakable. It would require almost a wilful attempt to misunderstand them.
This term-

He was talking about term 29.
-was passed by the parliament of the United Kingdom, House of Commons and House of Lords. It was passed by the parliament of Canada, House of Commons and Senate. It was confirmed by the government of the day in Newfoundland. That would be the commission of government. It forms part and parcel of Canada's constitution, the British North America Act of 1867 with amendments. It is therefore no ordinary document. It is not a contract made between two tradesmen. It is rather a solemn agreement made between two high contracting parties, these being the government of Newfoundland and the government of Canada at a time when they were separate countries.
What is term 29? The minister put it on the record once, but perhaps he will permit me and the committee will bear with me if I read it into my own remarks.
In view of the difficulty of predicting with sufficient accuracy the financial consequences to Newfoundland of becoming a province of Canada, the government of Canada will appoint a royal commission within eight years from the date of union to review the financial position of the province of Newfoundland and to recommend the form and scale of additional financial assistance, if any, that may be required-
May be required for what?
-by the government of the province of Newfoundland to enable it to continue public services at the levels and standards reached subsequent to the date of union, without resorting to taxation more burdensome, having regard to capacity to pay, than that obtaining generally in the region comprising the maritime provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.
I would just point out in regard to term 29 that there is no time limit in any way, shape or form, directly or indirectly; no time limit has been placed in this particular obligation.
Now, as the minister pointed out, in due course the royal commission to examine this matter of term 29 was appointed and it consisted, as he well said, of distinguished, competent, and I think objective persons who gave this problem the careful and considered examination to which it was entitled, and who made their report on May 31, 1958.
I agree with the minister that the matter under investigation was complicated. Indeed, the difficulties that faced this commission were only matched by their importance. There is no doubt about that. It was not easy, I am sure, for the commission to come to the conclusions that are embodied in its report. But I am perfectly certain that it did not come to those conclusions, and it did not make those recommendations, without a most exhaustive and painstaking examination, and without having received evidence from every possible source bearing on this problem.
This morning the minister put on the record some quotations from the report of the commission, and perhaps I may supplement one or two of them. He was quoting

from page 5 about the economic background of the immediate situation in Newfoundland. He quoted from the top paragraph on that page, or part of it, and I believe the last part of that paragraph should be added to what the minister said:
In this respect Newfoundland was at about the same stage as the maritime provinces were in 1867.
The minister himself put that sentence on the record. Then the report goes on to say:
The proportion of homes equipped with water and sewer services was only about one-third of the Canadian ratio. The death and disease rates were considerably higher than those in any other Canadian province, which indicated, among other things, a serious deficiency in health services. The physical facilities for education were generally inadequate.

The Prime Minister gave a broadcast in "The Nation's Business" series on April 20 and had this to say; I am quoting from the text of that broadcast:
I believe that the keystone of our union is the maintenance inviolate of the interpretation of those rights in terms of the fullest measure of equality of opportunity for all Canadians everywhere.

I have just given my own interpretation of what the minister said in general terms about the nature of the bill, and he can correct me if I am wrong. He suggested that there will be payments made for five years as recommended by the royal commission, and after that time the federal government will decide whether or not those payments are to be continued. In other words there is no obligation on the federal government to do anything after 1962 except to have the matter reconsidered before 1962. That seems to me to be contrary to the spirit of the obligation entered into by the federal government under article 29 of the terms of union.
The province can, the minister said, rely on the good will and understanding of the federal government to take all factors into consideration which have a bearing on the situation. The province of Newfoundland can rely on the federal government to do the right thing, but the province of Newfoundland has a stronger basis for action than just relying on the good will and understanding of the federal government, in our view. maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL GRANTS TO NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we in the C.C.F. group believe that Newfoundland has a very substantial claim for continuing grants from the federal treasury at such levels as will enable the province to maintain the level of services that has been reached in recent years without increasing their level of taxation beyond the general maritime level.
The objective, we feel, of national policy should be to raise the level of services all across our nation, but in particular the objective of national policy should be to increase the level of social services in the "have not" provinces. We believe it is essential in the context of our federal system that the federal government, which has such widespread taxing powers, should pay from general revenue to provincial governments by way of grants, moneys that will enable the residents of the "have not" provinces to enjoy substantially the same services that are maintained and enjoyed in the other provinces across this nation.
Anyone who has seen the province of Newfoundland will realize that levels of income and services in Canada's tenth province are definitely below the national average. As a matter of fact it is appalling to see many of the economic conditions that exist in that province. I refer to the lack of roads, and the housing that is below the standards that obtain in many other provinces. The general absence of prosperity and the appearance of prosperity as we see it in other provinces is very apparent.
During the few days I spent in Newfoundland last year I was given a very friendly reception and enjoyed meeting with the Canadian citizens of that province. Although I come from a province that has not enjoyed the same per capita income that has been enjoyed in some of the other provinces 1 was nevertheless shocked at what I saw of the economic conditions in Newfoundland. I remember being in one village where they were constructing some new streets and houses. The width of the new streets that were being surveyed, I was told, was just 50 feet. I asked why they would construct such a narrow street and was told that it was impossible to raise the funds necessary to provide wide, modern streets as we know them, for example, in the province of Ontario.
I believe that any member of this committee who has an interest in raising the standards of living for people in provinces where incomes are relatively low should support

substantial grants and adopt a generous outlook toward the problems of the people of N ewf oundland.
The members of the C.C.F. group, the party which forms the government today and the Liberal party which formed the government in 1949 supported the terms of union. Mr. M. J. Coldwell welcomed the entry of Newfoundland into confederation at that time as Canada's tenth province, and placed on the record our general objective that action by government at both levels should result in higher standards of living in the less well to do provinces. Mr. Coldwell, as reported on page 295 of Hansard for February, 7, 1949 had this to say:
May I say at once that members of the C.C.F. throughout Canada join with other people in welcoming into confederation the island of Newfoundland .. . We should consider Newfoundland and Labrador as part of the whole maritime region, which incidentally is a region that cries aloud for a new deal. . . We welcome Newfoundland, then, on another count; because it will tend to strengthen the position of the maritime provinces and the other "have not" provinces, and to highlight their problems.
Canadians generally believe today that Newfoundland's association with Canada in our confederation has been a very wise move and has been beneficial both to the citizens of Newfoundland and the citizens of the rest of Canada. But one would be blinding oneself if one did not recognize that in this addition to confederation and in the relations that have existed there have been substantial misunderstandings. I believe those misunderstandings have come about not entirely through the fault of either the government of Newfoundland or the federal government but because both in different instances have made some very serious mistakes. I believe the province of Newfoundland made a serious mistake in the labour laws it placed on its statute books recently which have resulted in the wiping out in certain instances of the freedom of association of workers in various trade unions for which they had previously indicated their support under the laws of that province. This action by the government of Newfoundland has not added to the cementing of the bonds of confederation.
The announcement made by the Prime Minister on March 25 last was another instance where the bonds of confederation were not tightened but rather were strained, having regard to the terms in which the announcement was couched. We think the terms of confederation are clear. There was to be a study by a royal commission to determine what federal assistance should continue in order that social services in the province of Newfoundland might be maintained at the level which had been reached without increasing taxes beyond the level of taxes in the

maritime provinces. This was surely a very minimum objective, because the level of services in the province of Newfoundland even after ten years of confederation is still substantially below the level of services in the rest of the maritime provinces. On page 8 of its report the royal commission had this to say on this point:
The construction programs have included significant outlays by the provincial government on industrial projects for economic development, on roads, on municipal works, and on education and health facilities. However, the expenditures on these items of social capital have served largely to keep up with the pace of a rapidly growing population. There have been few really major improvements in the levels and standards of services.
In the next paragraph the royal commission went on to say:
The lack of an adequate road system is, in the present day, one of the outstanding handicaps to economic development and social improvement.
And further:
The notable increases in Newfoundland production and incomes in recent years have not measurably reduced the disparities with the rest of the country which had previously existed. In the generally prosperous year of 1956 the average per capita personal income after adjustment for differences in the cost of living was still somewhat less than half the Canadian average and about one third less than that of the maritime provinces.
It is very obvious from the documentation of this report that services in Newfoundland are still below the maritime average, and that economic conditions in Newfoundland are not only inferior to the rest of the maritime provinces but much inferior to the remaining part of Canada. As has already been quoted a number of times in this debate, and it is not necessary to put the exact words on record again, the royal commission concludes that in order to fulfil the terms of union the federal government should pay to the province of Newfoundland after March 31, 1961 a sum of $8 million per annum. In the light of that recommendation the government has made a decision which was announced initially in the house on March 25. On that day the Prime Minister stated, as found on page 2216 of Hansard:
Notwithstanding the difficulties presented by its report, it remains a fact that the royal commission was appointed to fulfil the terms of union of Newfoundland with Canada, and these terms are part of the British North America Act. My colleagues and I are accordingly of the opinion that parliament should be invited to take action on the commission's recommendations. It is proposed, therefore, to ask parliament to authorize payments as recommended by the royal commission, but in our view the duration of the payments should be limited to five years-
The Prime Minister readily admits, as the royal commission finds in its report, that payment is necessary under the terms of union of 66968-9-375
Grants to Newfoundland Newfoundland and Canada, but he has not hesitated to say in the very same paragraph that by action of the federal government alone the implementing of these recommendations will cease as at March 31, 1962. The Prime Minister went on to say:
The proposed payments will be unconditional and will be in final and irrevocable settlement of the provisions of article 29 and the contractual obligations of the union consummated in 1949.
I think the Prime Minister erred gravely in making that latter statement. In the light of the objective that I feel all Canadians approve for the bringing of social services in the economically less fortunate provinces up to the level of services in other parts of Canada, in view of the fact that the history of this nation adequately demonstrates that the trend is for the federal government to pay more and more to the provinces to assist in the provision of essential services; and realizing that the trend in our economy is to expand, is there anyone here who believes that payments by the federal government to Newfoundland or to other provinces are likely to become less in the years ahead? So the suggestion in the Prime Minister's statement that this would be the end of the payments is not likely to be borne out by the facts. The fact is, I believe, and future events will prove this to be so, that increasing payments will be made to Newfoundland and other provinces. If that is what is most likely to happen, I think the Prime Minister's choice of words was unfortunate.
I can appreciate the position of the people of the province of Newfoundland. They have entered confederation and become a part of our nation in recent years. They are not fully conscious of the background of our nation. They feel that the guarantee they have as to economic conditions in the years ahead is contained in the terms of union, and the terms of union being further carried out have brought forth a royal commission recommendation which says, in simple English, that after the initial period spelled out, grants from the federal government shall be $8 million per annum.
I can understand their feeling that the government of Canada had sabotaged their terms of confederation when the Prime Minister announced that, in final and irrevocable settlement of the provisions of article 29, payments would be made to the end of March 31, 1962. They do not understand, as I think members of all political parties in this house really understand, that this kind of obligation of the central government to all the provinces is one that is continuing and will continue. In the light of the statement by the Prime Minister and their short history as part of Canada, I can understand why they

Grants to Newfoundland felt this was a black day for the province of Newfoundland, and why the announcement would indicate for them that it was a day of mourning.
The government has taken into account, in some measure, the feeling of the people of the province of Newfoundland. They have announced that they are putting in the bill that will be introduced a special clause which says there will be further consideration of the position of Newfoundland by March 31, 1962. This is going some distance in taking into account the very natural feelings of the people of Newfoundland. Any federal statute that has within it a provision for the payment of a certain sum of money to a provincial government cannot, I think, be reasonably considered something that is there for all time. After all, it is the prerogative of the members of the House of Commons, of parliament, to amend Canadian statutes from time to time, and to amend those statutes which have in them provisions for certain payments, under certain conditions, and that are placed there on an indefinite basis.
I come to the conclusion, therefore, that in considering the recommendation of the royal commission that a grant of $8 million per annum should be paid thereafter, the federal government, in order to implement this recommendation, should have provided exactly what the recommendation says, namely for the payment of $8 million per annum to Newfoundland. This does not mean that $8 million, $8 million alone and nothing more, will remain in that statute forever. It merely means that is what the people of Newfoundland can look for on an indefinite basis until such time as the parliament of Canada, in its wisdom, decides to amend the provision.
I want to say, Mr. Chairman, that although we in the C.C.F. group have taken strong exception, and will continue to take strong exception, to certain actions of the government of Newfoundland which we have felt interfered with basic human rights and fundamental freedoms of Canadian citizens in Newfoundland, this in no way colours our attitude toward the economic case for Newfoundland or to the terms of confederation when they are under consideration. I feel it is a sorry day not only for Newfoundland but for all of Canada when there is so much misunderstanding over the grants that are paid to Newfoundland under the terms of confederation. I would think that a province like Newfoundland, coming into a new nation and accepting its obligations, should expect from any federal government in this country the maximum amount of consultation, the 
maximum amount of consideration. If there were this kind of consideration by both the federal and provincial government there would be no violent controversy as to whether or not the terms of union have been implemented.
I would suggest that, in keeping with the terms of reference, in keeping with the objectives of the Canadan nation, the federal government should act in such a way as to provide grants and assistance to Newfoundland, to the other maritime provinces and to the other provinces, that would provide financial help at such levels as would enable Canadian citizens from one coast of this nation to the other to enjoy substantially the same social services.

Mr. Chairman, I was glad to hear the hon. member for Assiniboia say that the Newfoundland labour legislation has no relevance to this debate because I, too, regard it as irrelevant and for that reason I do not intend to make any reference whatever to it.
The purpose of introducing a resolution before a money bill must be to get the feeling of the house as to what the bill should contain. The wording of this particular resolution does less than justice to the bill that will be introduced if this resolution carries, because it makes reference only to provision for the payment of additional grants to Newfoundland, and makes no reference whatever to the fact that these payments are made as a constitutional right under the terms of union.
The bill that will be introduced after this resolution passes is not just another money bill to provide financial assistance to a needy province. The sums of money and payments specified in this bill are of a very special nature because they represent, in tangible form, one of the most important conditions under which Newfoundland agreed to forgo its own national sovereignty and become the tenth province of the Dominion of Canada.
These payments represent one of the constitutional rights of the province of Newfoundland, a constitutional right which is embodied in a solemn treaty between the people of Newfoundland and the people of Canada. This morning the minister went to some pains to point out that there was no legal obligation binding the government of Canada to make these payments, but he did admit that there was a moral obligation. Well, Mr. Chairman, are we to assume that a moral obligation is less binding than a legal obligation? Let there be no misunderstanding on this point. These payments represent a treaty obligation, and the amount

and manner in which they are paid constitute an indication and a means by which the good faith of the mainland Canadians, on whose behalf they are made, can be measured.
These payments are to be made in accordance with term 29 of the act of union. When a sovereign country sacrifices its sovereignty and forfeits its chief sources of revenue, great financial adjustments must of necessity be involved. It was beyond human wisdom and capability to forecast with any degree of accuracy what financial impact confederation with Canada would have upon Newfoundland generally, and particularly upon revenues available to the provincial government. It was for that reason that term 29 was inserted in the terms of union. So union with Canada became largely an act of faith on the part of the Newfoundland people, faith in term 29 and in the integrity of the people of mainland Canada.
As the minister pointed out this morning, term 29 provides for a review of the financial position of Newfoundland within eight years from the date of union, and it makes the following provisions. In the first place, it postpones a final settlement indefinitely and it directs that a royal commission be set up within eight years to do certain things. It also directs that royal commission to review the financial position of the province of Newfoundland and to recommend the form and scale of additional financial assistance, if any, that may be required by the government of the province of Newfoundland to enable it to do certain things having regard to certain conditions.
What was it that the Newfoundland government was to be enabled to do? Term 29 is very clear on this point. The Newfoundland government was to be enabled to continue public services at the levels and standards reached subsequent to the date of union, that is the levels and standards reached in 1957, eight years after the date of union. What was the limiting factor which would determine the size of payments and the conditions under which payments, if any were recommended, would be made? Again term 29 is perfectly clear. The limiting factor is that Newfoundland is to be enabled to continue these services at the 1957 level without resorting to taxation more burdensome, having regard to capacity to pay, than that obtaining in the maritime provinces generally.
Hon. members must bear in mind the fact that Newfoundland came into confederation 80 years late. Because of that fact Newfoundland did not enjoy the benefits of confederation which had been available to the mainland provinces for a period of some 80 years.
