Grants to Newfoundland Newfoundland has never at any time enjoyed as much prosperity as have the other maritime provinces of Canada, a prosperity which was due largely to their huge ship-building and shipping industry and which continued after confederation though at a much slower rate.
Consequently, at the time of confederation with Canada in 1949 the public services of Newfoundland-health services, hospitals, roads, schools, etc.-were about 50 years behind those of the maritime provinces. On becoming a part of Canada the provincial government, under the dynamic leadership of Premier Smallwood, put forth a concentrated effort to improve those services. Because she had been left to her own resources, dependent upon a precarious fishing industry as the mainstay of her economy; because she had been handicapped by severe laws passed in order to discourage colonization and to encourage exploitation by the English merchants; because she had been disappointed time and time again by apathy in the mother country; because she had been faced with fires, famine, financial crisis, catastrophes, and tragedies, Newfoundland had never been in a position to build up a high level of public services.
During the first eight years of confederation more roads were built, more classrooms were constructed, more hospital beds were provided than in all our previous history. But in spite of these prodigious efforts, at the time of the royal commission inquiry in 1957 our public services were still 25 years behind those of the maritime provinces, and the public services of the maritime provinces are themselves considerably below those of central and western Canada.
The purpose, then, of these payments under term 29 is to enable the public services of Newfoundland to be continued at a level which is at least 25 years behind that of the maritime provinces, provided this cannot be done by the Newfoundland government without resorting to taxation more burdensome than that of the other maritime provinces.
Hon. members must be quite clear as to the difference between payments made under term 29, which we are considering in this resolution, and payments made under the Atlantic provinces grants act. Reports and articles in the mainland press indicate a great deal of confusion in the public mind on this point. It has been intimated that the grants are similar, that they serve the same purpose and can be substituted the one for the other. Nothing could be further from the truth. They are quite different in nature, they serve different purposes and are paid under different conditions.

Grants to Newfoundland
Payments made under the bill which will be introduced as a result of this resolution and which embodies term 29 are made as a matter of right. It is our safeguard, our guarantee that our levels and standards of public services will never be permitted to fall below what they were in 1957. It was on the basis of that guarantee that Newfoundland agreed to become a part of Canada, and Newfoundland can claim these payments as a constitutional right whenever and as long as she is unable to continue her public services at the 1957 level without resorting to taxation more burdensome than that which obtained in the maritime provinces at the same time.
Payments made under the Atlantic provinces grants act are not made as a matter of right but by the grace and favour of the government of the day. That is a very important difference. Equally important is the difference in purpose. The purpose of the payments under term 29 is to continue the public services of Newfoundland at their 1957 level. I should like to stress the word "continue". To continue the same level of public services for an increasing population means a yearly increase in public expenditures which cannot be satisfied by fixed grants even if dollar depreciation were not an important factor.
In contrast, the purpose of payments under the Atlantic provinces grants act is to enable the different provinces to improve their levels and standards of public services. If federal funds are to be devoted to the improvement of provincial public services, surely Newfoundland is entitled to share in that improvement. Indeed, on the basis of need Newfoundland would have a prior claim because her need is greater than that of the others. Otherwise the effect of the Atlantic provinces grants would be to widen the gap between Newfoundland and the other maritime provinces in their levels and standards of public services beyond the 25 years which is the case at the present time.
It cannot be denied that funds made available to the Newfoundland government through the Atlantic provinces grants, through tax rental agreements and other financial agreements, in so far as they contribute to the general revenue and affect the level of taxation in the province will have an important bearing on the size of payments made under term 29. It is true also that Newfoundland possesses a great potential of natural wealth which, when developed, will also improve her revenue position and tax burden.
We look forward to the day-and it may not be very far in the future-when Newfoundland will, through her own resources, be able to continue her public services at


the 1957 level without a tax burden any heavier than that of other maritime provinces. When that day arrives, and as long as that condition continues, Newfoundland will have no claims for financial assistance under term 29. But that does not mean that the agreement under term 29 is terminated. That agreement is part of our constitution, and it must remain as long as our constitution lasts. It may become temporarily inoperative-we hope it will become permanently inoperative- but it must never be terminated because it is our guarantee of a minimum level and standard of public service; it is our only safeguard against a return in the future of those misfortunes which too often in the past have been our lot.
I therefore plead with the minister to insert in the bill that will be introduced later a provision to safeguard Newfoundland's constitutional right and to honour the solemn agreement with Newfoundland entered into in 1949.

Mr. Chairman, I had intended to make some rather extended remarks on this resolution, but following the statement made by the Minister of Finance this morning and having heard some of the general terms of the bill, there seems to me to be little purpose in discussing the resolution in detail when we already know in general terms what the bill is going to be.
My leader has placed our position on record, and it appears to me now that the comments I might have made at the resolution stage might more properly be made when the bill is before the house. However, there is one point which I think we ought to get clear and it is this. Term 29 is not an agreement between a province of Canada and the federal government. Term 29 is a solemn agreement between two sovereign nations and, in my opinion, has nothing at all to do with the fiscal relations existing between the province and the dominion. It was an agreement entered into before Newfoundland became a province of Canada and, may I say, it was an agreement which played a large part in Newfoundland becoming a province of Canada.
I suggest to you today, Mr. Chairman, that if term 29 had not been one of the terms of union with Newfoundland, I doubt very much whether we would be discussing this bill here today.
I know from my own people back in Newfoundland that one of the things which made the terms of union agreeable to them was the fact that after a period of eight years it would be possible to have this matter reviewed and to do something about maintaining the levels of services which had been reached at the end of the eight years. I say

again that term 29 is not an agreement between the federal government and the province; it is an agreement between two sovereign, independent nations and one which I think this government has nothing else to do but to honour. If that agreement is going to be broken or if there is going to be a change in the agreement, I think that change should be after consultation between the federal government of Canada and the now province of Newfoundland. It was an agreement entered into by two parties, and I believe it should not be changed other than by agreement between the two parties.
In the report of the McNair commission there can surely be no misunderstanding of this recommendation. There can be no misunderstanding at all as to what the recommendation means. I had hoped the time would come when my province would be able to play a more independent part in the Canadian federation that it has played in the last ten years, and I believe that it will. I believe that the time will come when we can develop our province to the point where it will be far less dependent upon the federal government than it is today. But that is going to take time, and it will need support and it will need money. However, I still believe that although we are the newest and the youngest province of Canada, the time will come when we will be able to make a substantial contribution to the Canadian federation. Our natural resources when properly developed will bring not only income to the people of Newfoundland but will bring income to the federal government. If our people are permitted to become Canadians I have no doubt there will be none more loyal except perhaps those who have always had the privilege of calling themselves Canadians.
Mr. Chairman, I listened to the speech made by the hon. member for Assiniboia. I sincerely regret that it was necessary for him to describe the province from which I come in the terms he did, but I must agree with him. We do need in Newfoundland many more improvements in our services if we are to bring the level of our services up even to the levels which are enjoyed by the people of the three maritime provinces. In the field of education we are having a difficult time, not only in improving the standard as it is now but even in maintaining it. In a province where a great many of the people are settled around the shores in isolated settlements, education becomes a mighty expensive service. Some years ago I had the opportunity of comparing the system of education in Newfoundland with that in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario, and even today I must admit that our services
Grants to Newfoundland are far below the services that are given to the young people of these other provinces.
Of course, that is not true in every place in Newfoundland. In my own city the educational services are perhaps a little higher than on the coast. That may be true for other larger centres in Newfoundland as well; but generally speaking the standards of education in Newfoundland require a great deal of improvement, and it will take a lot of support to be able to do that.
Our health services are at a much lower level than those experienced by people here on the mainland. In my own home city there exists a hospital that was built with some assistance from the provincial government, and by a large donation from the public in general. When that hospital was built it was well able to serve the needs of the area, but that is no longer so. Today the hospital is not able to provide the medical attention which an ordinary Canadian expects and deserves in this day and age.
One might also go on and mention other levels of services. On an earlier occasion in the house during this session, as I have in other sessions, I referred to transportation in Newfoundland and to the tremendous load which is placed upon Newfoundlanders in being asked to build their share of the trans-Canada highway. For example, the number of miles per 10,000 of population, regardless of the difficulty in building, regardless of cost, and regardless of the ability to pay, is still twice as much as in any other province, and is roughly four times that which exists in the province of Ontario. Certainly the need is great, and I hope that when this bill is introduced it will give to us something of a different conception than that given to us by the Minister of Finance this morning. If it does not, let me assure you, Mr. Chairman, that Newfoundlanders will be a very disappointed people. They will be angered, for they will feel that once again history, as it has so many times in the past, has worked against them, and I am sure they will feel that not the Canadian people but the Canadian government has deliberately failed to honour an agreement between the people of the province of Newfoundland and the central government of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, there have been many important items raised affecting the province of Newfoundland, both on the floor of the house and outside the house, in the recent past. They were items very controversial in their purport, and were subjects of far-reaching concern to the province of Newfoundland, indeed to this Dominion of Canada. I must confess that as a Newfoundlander I have found some of the points

Grants to Newfoundland of view expressed inside and outside this house, and some of the decisions taken because of those points of view, a little difficult to reconcile. At the same time, I fully recognize the constitutional responsibilities of those placed in positions of authority.
Perhaps of all the questions to be discussed in this house and outside, none is more important to Newfoundland than that outlined in the resolution which is now under discussion, namely article 29 of the terms of union. Indeed, article 29 is the whole purpose of this debate today, and underlies our discussion. Article 29 was born out of the contract of union between Newfoundland and Canada. As has been outlined earlier today, Mr. Chairman, article 29 called for the establishment of a royal commission some eight years after union. That article has been quoted by the Minister of Finance and by others in its entirety, and I will not burden the house with undue repetition. However, we must not lose sight of one important fact, namely that as has been established clearly here today article 29 called for the setting up of a royal commission, and in my opinion it has placed certain obligations upon us. But there is one inescapable fact, and it is this: royal commissions may recommend, but they may never legislate; the sole body which may legislate is this parliament.
I was naturally interested, and I may say a little concerned, on going back through the debates of the House of Commons leading up to confederation in 1949 to find that so little reference was made to article 29, particularly in committee. One of the few references I could find was the reference by the then prime minister which has been quoted by the Minister of Finance and which is to be found on page 289 of Hansard of 1949. Perhaps one should not lose sight of that point, the fact that article 29 was perfectly clear to everybody in 1949 and prior to 1949 when it was adopted in this house.
What of the royal commission itself? We have heard many quotations read by hon. members who have preceded me from the report of the royal commission dealing with various economic factors in the province of Newfoundland. However, we have heard little reference to the failure of that royal commission to discharge one of the most important functions under article 29, namely to establish a scale. To my mind, this is where the royal commission fails-it failed to establish a scale of financial assistance. The royal commission bases its conclusions on its findings with regard to economic conditions in the province as they are now and as they were eight years ago. I should like to quote from the report of the royal commission on page 5. It says:

The need to improve social services and health and educational facilities laid a heavy claim upon the provincial revenues. This claim was always in conflict with the need to achieve economic betterment. Under these conditions the provincial government sought out and resorted to short cuts. A considerable attempt was made to achieve a quick increase in employment opportunities through the establishment of secondary manufacturing industries with the aid of provincial loans and credits. Financial assistance was also given for the construction of a number of plants to process local natural resources. Substantial credits were made available to achieve a rapid increase in fish-processing facilities. To a considerable extent these direct financial commitments were undertaken at the expense of greater progress in the provision of basic facilities and services. Apparently, in the face of immediate employment problems it was thought that there was no time to waste for longer-run but more lasting results. In the event, these measures have met with a mixed and sometimes transitory success.
The conclusions to be drawn from this are evident, and I will not go into them here because they would bring in topics of a controversial provincial-political nature. After all, reference was made in the report as the minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Assiniboia pointed out, to what is perhaps one of the greatest shortcomings in Newfoundland today, namely the lack of an adequate road system. The minister quoted from page 4 of the royal commission's report and I will not go into that aspect of the question here. However, at page 8 there is another reference to this particular shortcoming, roads and it reads as follows:
The lack of an adequate road system is, in the present day, one of the outstanding handicaps to economic development and social improvement. From the economic standpoint this basic deficiency is a serious obstacle to a better concentration of population; it hinders the development of natural resources, raises the costs of distribution, restricts the diversification of industry and limits the growth of local enterprise. From the social standpoint the lack of roads adds substantially to the cost and difficulty of providing a necessary and desirable standard of public services. In short, Newfoundland is confronted with the urgent tasks of modernization, but is without the modern means of mobility and communication.
This factor is also referred to in the Gordon report or the report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, and the quotation which I should like to read can be found at page 408 of that report:
It was made clear to us that perhaps Newfoundland's greatest single need was a greatly expanded system of roads in order to open up the resources of the province and also to establish communication between the centres of population and at least some of the potentially more accessible outports.
If the report of the McNair commission does not do anything more than highlight some of the deficiencies in Canada's overseas province, it will achieve a great deal as far as the economic development of the

Atlantic coast is concerned. I am sure that hon. members are not fully aware of how important this road shortage is. Most hon. members of this committee have never visited the province of Newfoundland and indeed many government members have not visited there. I would suggest that steps be taken in the future to see that there is a greater familiarity with Canada's newest province, this least known area of Canada. If hon. members were to go there they would, as the hon. member for Assiniboia pointed out, see how apparent is this deficiency in a system of roads.
I wish to make a comparison. My figures may be questioned because it is extremely difficult to find accurate figures with regard to road mileage. According to the statistics I have, the province of Newfoundland with the territory of Labrador represents a land mass of 152,000 square miles and has a total road mileage of 7,101 miles as against the province of Nova Scotia with an area of only 21,068 square miles and a total road mileage of 15,257. The implications of this analysis are obvious.
Equally obvious is the fact that under the present arrangement Newfoundland lacks the financial resources which would enable it to live up to its obligations under the Trans-Canada Highway Act and to provide provincial access roads. It has been estimated that to build and finish the trans-Canada highway in Newfoundland would cost $80 million. Nowhere else in Canada, I suggest, is there a road problem such as there is in Newfoundland nowhere else in this country has the lack of roads retarded progress to the extent it has there.
Another aspect dealt with in the McNair commission report which is highly important and one concerning which not enough is heard is the extreme vulnerability-and I underline the words "extreme vulnerability", -of the Newfoundland economy. We are at the very end of the economic yard stick. If there is a minor recession in North America, in Newfoundland it comes closer to being a full scale depression and indeed serious problems arose last year as a result of the North American economic recession. The vulnerability of the economy of the newest province is due to many factors, not the least of which is an economy based primarily on export trade, a false economy, referred to at page 7 of the McNair report in these words:
The heavy dependence in recent years upon the construction industry has introduced a further source of instability. In the best of times, it is a highly seasonal industry. Consequently seasonal unemployment and underemployment have continued to be major problems and important factors in the low level of annual incomes. Furthermore
Grants to Newfoundland the rate of construction activity is subject to wide fluctuations in accordance with business conditions and market developments as they affect an export economy. Throughout the period 1949-56 the magnitudes of the construction programs in Newfoundland whether for military purposes or resource development, have from year to year dominated the economic scene to a greater extent than in other regions of Canada.
This present year we in Newfoundland are experiencing a boom in the building industry, but what happens the year after that when these buildings are completed? What happens the year after that when there is no more building and there is a famine in the fishery? I say that these are serious questions requiring serious and careful attention and consideration lest we see in Canada's newest province a repetition of what happened in the early thirties. That is why it is so important for us to have the wherewithal to develop our own resources, to develop the resources of the great Labrador storehouse, a natural storehouse of untold mineral wealth, and the forests and minerals of the island of Newfoundland proper.
Another aspect touched on by the McNair commission which has not been mentioned in this debate thus far and which to my mind is worthy of consideration is this. I quote from page 12 of the report:
Because of the very limited development of municipal institutions, the provincial revenues in Newfoundland were required to cover the cost of services which in other provinces are generally paid for out of municipal taxes-
In other words the municipalities in Newfoundland are unable through their own sources of revenue to provide the basic services that municipalities in other parts of Canada are expected to provide. Again this represents a tremendous drain on the finances of the Newfoundland government.
The vulnerability of the Newfoundland economy to which I referred a moment ago was clearly spelled out in the report of the royal commission at page 40 where it is stated:
The economy of Newfoundland is highly vulnerable and is somewhat more dependent upon export industries than is the economy of the maritime provinces. For this reason the provincial and municipal revenues in Newfoundland may be subject to greater variation. The amount of accumulated capital and wealth is noticeably smaller in Newfoundland than in the maritime provinces. Average per capita money incomes, after the exemptions we have allowed in our calculations, are lower. This difference in incomes is greater in real terms because of the higher cost of living in Newfoundland-
These are some of the problems highlighted by the McNair report and very obvious to those people who are familiar with Newfoundland. There is on the order paper notice of motion with respect to encouraging

Grants to Newfoundland industry in the Atlantic provinces. I should like to refer for a moment, just as a recommendation to be considered perhaps at some future date, to a statute on the books of the parliament at Westminster passed in 1945 and known as the distribution of industry act, 1945. This legislation was primarily designed to provide long term loans at low interest rates to establish industries in those areas of the United Kingdom which do not have, by comparison, the means to provide jobs. This act was amended in 1950 and again in 1958, widening its original intent and broadening its scope. I would commend similar legislation for those economically depressed regions of Canada of which Newfoundland is one. On April 13, 1959, referring to the need to encourage industry and develop resources, the Newfoundland board of trade, an organization known in Newfoundland for many years, sent an open letter to the Prime Minister. I should like to quote from that letter as it is apropos to my remarks concerning the United Kingdom distribution of industry act. It reads in part as follows:
From the beginning of this century, until relatively recent times, the policy of the federal government was to develop the resources of Canada by extension of the frontiers and by assistance to private enterprise. This policy took the form of advancing and fostering settlement, creating a transportation system across the nation, encouraging manufacturing industries by tariff protection and other means; the construction of highways, canals, harbour developments, docks and terminals, public buildings and utilities of various kinds. Newfoundland, of course, was not part of Canada through all this process, and relatively little economic development took place; the island during that time depending on the export market for the sale of our primary produce and the cost of living in Newfoundland being kept artificially high by a substantial revenue tariff.
The letter goes on to refer to the fact that Newfoundland joined Canada in the era of social security and that while this is desirable and helpful it must not be allowed to become a substitute for productive, wealth-creating work which can only come as a result of developing our primary resources to the full.
I realize, Mr. Chairman, that I have been broad in my remarks but I feel that the onus is on me not only to draw attention to these deficiencies in our economy but as a responsible member of the house to suggest some means of overcoming these deficiencies. I think that in my remarks there is at least some suggestion of how these problems might be overcome through the necessary research and investigation.
I would quote from the remarks made by the Prime Minister on April 20 of this year on the national television network program "The Nation's Business". The Prime Minister, in referring to Newfoundland at that time, had this to say:

In the case of Newfoundland, there has, I am sorry to say, been some misunderstanding-but differences arise even in the best of families. Let me say at once that I believe that we can and will resolve these differences in that spirit of understanding, common sense and compromise which has been so characteristic of the Canadian confederation from its very beginning. While there is a difference of opinion at the moment about the interpretation of specific terms, what is much more important is that there should be neither doubt nor misunderstanding about the equality of Newfoundland's status in the Canadian partnership.
He emphasized the full equality of Newfoundland's status in the Canadian partnership. I do not wish to refer to personalities in any controversial way because I do not approve of that but for a moment I should like to refer to the words of the premier of Newfoundland uttered in Ottawa on April 8 of this year. The premier said at that time, and I quote from a press dispatch, that Canada "would resume its role of ignoring Newfoundland as it has done for 10 years". "As it has done for 10 years", and for the first eight years of confederation hon. gentlemen opposite were in office at Ottawa.
As has been pointed out already today, we in Newfoundland have the highest birth rate and the lowest death rate in all of Canada. At the same time we only produce 10 per cent of the province's estimated food requirements. It is this fact, coupled with the high cost of transportation, that gives Canada's tenth province the highest cost of living in the dominion. When this fact is compared with the very frightening statistic that we also have the lowest per capita income in the dominion, then the conclusions to be drawn go without saying. Always in Newfoundland we have had the problem of the people of that old and ancient colony fighting against difficult odds, always struggling against the spectre of poverty. This has been our lot down through the years and it is only of recent date with the promise of development of our great natural resources that we have shown some signs of achieving that degree of stability in our economy so essential to our own well-being.
I should like to refer for a moment to the statement of the Minister of Finance. In speaking of the bill he said that it expressly states in one of the recitals that any special circumstances relating to the financial position of the province of Newfoundland after March 31, 1962 will be taken into consideration. Although I have not seen the bill, I think some of the economic background and the economic circumstances and difficulties in Newfoundland have been clearly spelled out in the bill in the light of the reference to it by the Minister of Finance. I feel satisfied that after 1962 the special needs of Newfoundland will be given that consideration

in keeping with the spirit of confederation. Who can tell whether at that time that consideration of this factor may or may not be an important factor?
The real issue underlying all the controversies, underlying term 29, underlying this resolution, underlying this debate, is not the payments that have been made in the past or the payments that are now being made but the future. What of the future? This to my mind is the crux of the matter, the future of Canada's newest province within the framework of confederation, the ability of the Newfoundland people to achieve a standard equitable with the standard taken for granted by Canadians in other parts of this great country. No one will question the fact that Newfoundland, like other provinces, will have to depend in large measure on fiscal payments from the federal government in order to develop resources and improve services. But in this way we will be adding to the development of Canada as a whole.
I believe it rather unfortunate that both inside this chamber and outside suggestions have been made that payments to Newfoundland will abruptly end in 1962. I take exception to those statements, and I further submit that this is a most unrealistic attitude, particularly from those people who have had experience in federal-provincial relations. I note also with considerable regret that during the controversies of recent months there have been many attacks of a personal nature upon the Prime Minister and members of the government by those people who purport to be responsible leaders in Newfoundland. I want to assure the Prime Minister and the members of this government-I feel I can speak on behalf of the great majority of Newfoundlanders-that these attacks of a personal nature are merely the narrow partisan views of a few and they in no way reflect the true feelings of the Newfoundland people.
I regret to have to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.
If the committee would give me a few minutes more, I would be able to finish.
Oh, certainly.

Is it
the pleasure of hon. members to allow the hon. member to continue?
Agreed.

I was saying that these narrow partisan views are merely a reflection of the views of a few, and in no way characterize the view of the people of Newfoundland as a whole. Throughout their long
Grants to Newfoundland history the people of Newfoundland have always, and in all places, manifested the highest respect for men in high office. Furthermore, the people of Newfoundland are not at all unaware of the record of achievement of this government, particularly as it applies to the Atlantic region and, indeed, as it applies to the province of Newfoundland.
Finally, may I say that a chain is only as strong as its weakest link and so, too, is this nation only as rich as its poorest province. In the words of my colleague from Halifax spoken in this house, we believe that government exists for the people and not the people for government. Underlying all the controversies are the people of Newfoundland and their disabilities. If they have disabilities,
I am the less as a fellow Canadian.

Mr. Chairman, the statement of the Prime Minister made last March was unfavourably received in Newfoundland and also in many parts of Canada. I am sure that the announcement of the Minister of Finance today will be received with even greater disappointment. The minister said all Canadians welcomed the union. Of course they did. He also said that we entered union in a spirit of fairness on both sides. With this statement, I am sure all Newfoundlanders will agree.
He referred also to the word "thereafter" in the report of the royal commission on Newfoundland finances, and how it could be applied. I want to assure this committee that it only has one meaning so far as Newfoundlanders are concerned and that is, as it states, thereafter or until the government of Newfoundland and the federal government meet to discuss or review the terms of union. When Newfoundland entered confederation her entry was different from the entry of the other provinces because the result was a union between two sovereign states under the British crown, even though Newfoundland's sovereignty was temporarily suspended.
When the terms of union were signed they bound the governments of the future to carry out those terms, and the parliament of that day confirmed that obligation by a formal act of parliament approving the terms of union. An amendment was made to the British North America Act which made the terms of union a part of the constitution of Canada. It was Prime Minister Mackenzie King's opinion that if Newfoundland did not join Canada she would join with the United States, and ultimately confederation itself would be endangered if its eastern gateway were to be dominated by a foreign power.
When Newfoundlanders finally faced the issue and voted by a small majority to join
5920	HOUSE OF
Grants to Newfoundland Canada, Prime Minister Mackenzie King was very disappointed with the slight majority. The final negotiations for union were left to Prime Minister St. Laurent, but Prime Minister King had fulfilled Macdonald's vision of a nation taking in the north half of the continent. Thus it was under the late Prime Minister Mackenzie King that confederation was completed.
Under the terms of union a royal commission was to be appointed within eight years of the date of union, and while the terms do not say that any parliament had to accept the recommendations of that commission, few Newfoundlanders thought the government would not carry out in good faith the constitutional obligation to provide additional financial assistance, if any were required, to enable the government of Newfoundland to continue the levels of provincial services without greater provincial taxes than the average in the maritimes. It was also the belief that the constitutional obligation was not to end in 1962, or any other year. It was to last as long as the union lasted, just as the constitutional subsidies to other provinces were to continue as long as confederation continued.
I was shocked at the announcement of the Minister of Finance of the decision of the Progressive Conservative government on term 29 of the terms of union of Newfoundland with Canada. In my opinion, the recommendations of the McNair commission were the lowest possible that could, with honour, be offered to Newfoundland under term 29. I am convinced also that neither those who signed the terms of union 10 years ago nor the McNair commission ever recommended or even envisaged the stoppage of this grant after a definite period.
The Diefenbaker government, after twelve months considering the recommendations of the McNair commission and term 29, accepted the recommendations of this commission only as a yardstick to back up their decision and then by limiting the grant to only five years duration. I hope Mr. Chairman, that this does not show any political spleen toward the Newfoundland government or the Newfoundland premier who has the courage of his convictions and who has never been afraid to speak out whenever the welfare of Newfoundland or its people were at stake.
In my opinion, the government of Canada has lost face by this act of betrayal in failing to honour a sacred bond given and accepted in good faith just 10 years ago. The honour and record of Canada as a nation has been defamed and blackened in the nations of the world and unless and until this decision is voided or adjusted the word of Canada will 

never again be accepted with sincerity and confidence. This is a sad period in the history of Canada, when her honour and integrity have been blackened by the betrayal decision of a Progressive Conservative government which a short time ago won acclaim unequalled in political history based on promises of sincerity, integrity and fair dealings in all matters affecting Canada and Canadians. Today, by the decision of the Diefenbaker government in not honouring the sacred word given just over 10 years ago, Newfoundland has been betrayed and Canada stands before the nations of the world as a country which has betrayed her province. Canadians everywhere will deeply resent this blackening of their country's honour. I now conclude with a verse from our ode to Newfoundland:
As loved our fathers, so we love,
Where once they stood we stand,
Their prayer we raise to Heaven above God guard thee, Newfoundland.

Mr. Chairman, in common, I believe, with virtually all of Newfoundland and, I would dare to say, most Canadians, I was deeply shocked this morning by the announcement of the Minister of Finance with regard to the final part of the confederation of Newfoundland with Canada. Term 29, which has been debated here today, was an act of faith on the part of the people of Newfoundland when they decided to join their destiny with the destiny of the great nation of Canada. The interpretation put upon term 29 this morning seems, to me at least, to be the negation of the spirit of that time. Indeed, it seems to contain the seeds of disunity and the fear of oppression.
Term 29 is distinct and clear from the other grants which have been made to Newfoundland. The grant to the Atlantic provinces was designed to help those provinces which were considered to be less prosperous than the rest of Canada. But term 29 was designed to help Newfoundland maintain the improved standards which it was hoped the province would have at this later date. Since Newfoundland entered confederation 10 years ago a great many improvements have been made in the public utilities of Newfoundland including roads, schools and hospitals. All these have been improved. I imagine that in the past 10 years more progress has been made than in previous history. However, this was done at high cost in effort and in money.
The maintenance of these improved services is what term 29 was designed to cover. Having obtained these improvements, having had more and better schools, more and better roads and more and better hospitals, how are we to maintain them if term 29 is not to be implemented in its original meaning? That meaning was clear. Ten years ago the

government of the day and the Newfoundland people tried, as far as possible, to protect the future of Newfoundland. No one could forecast that far into the future but what they could do was to make sure that means were available by which adjustments, such as time and circumstance should determine, might be made. This in essence was term 29, and it was left to the future years for those who at that future time were the guardians of Canada's destiny and honour, to implement the intent of the people who wrote and signed that agreement. But the limited interpretation put upon term 29 this morning has jeopardized the whole future of our province. After the interpretation put upon the word "thereafter", what reason is there for us to have much faith in the phrase "special needs"? Today there is small reason to blame the people of my province for feeling that they have been betrayed.
Shall the resolution carry?
Does the minister from Newfoundland not intend to speak?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What about?
Carried.
Shall the resolution carry?

No, Mr. Chairman. If the minister is without voice, as he has been throughout the consideration of this matter up to now, I as the one remaining member from Newfoundland who has not yet spoken will certainly not be without voice.
Oh, oh.

At the same time, I do not intend to take a great deal of time in the committee this afternoon on this matter. I myself think that there is only one point that really divides the government and the opposition. That point was put with great clarity by the leader of our party and it has been successively put by each of the members on this side of the house from Newfoundland. It is in order to indicate our unanimity of view on this matter as much as anything else that I too am going to take a little of the time of the committee.
The hon. member for St. John's East made one or two observations but he carefully avoided discussing term 29 or what it meant. He seemed to express contentment with an enunication of some hazy and pious aspiration on the part of the Minister of Finance that there would be some vague clause in the bill indicating that special circumstances would be taken into account in 1962. We would never have had any of these fiscal
Grants to Newfoundland arrangements between the federal and provincial governments which have been characteristic of the period since the second world war if it had not been for the inexorable need, because of the nature of our federal system, of special consideration for special situations. If all the provinces had the same levels of income and the same resources there would be no need for tax-sharing arrangements at all. Everyone could stand on his own feet. What the minister is saying, as clearly as we can see it without having the bill before us, is that Newfoundland is to lose a right under the constitution and in substitution thereof is to be given the same kind of consideration, or lack of consideration, that may or may not be given before 1962.
The minister said in response to a question of mine, when I asked him what statutory authority he had for saying that these tax sharing arrangements must be reviewed before 1962, that there was no statutory obligation. And there is no statutory obligation. There is no "must" at all. It all depends on the grace of this government, this government which in November, 1957 undertook to call a federal-provincial conference in January, 1958 and did not carry out that promise but imposed a unilateral arrangement. There is no reason, on the basis of the experience we have had with this government, to expect anything except unilateral treatment of the provinces in 1962. As my hon. friend from Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador has just said, when we get the extraordinary distortion of the ordinary, plain English meaning of the word "thereafter" which we have already got from the Minister of Finance this morning, there is certainly no reason to expect that we will get anything whatsoever beyond what this government unilaterally is willing to do in 1962 or before 1962.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to make one or two observations about one or two of the points which were made by the Minister of Finance this morning before making my own brief contribution to this debate. First of all I want to say that I was disappointed, and I know the people of Newfoundland will also be disappointed, that it was the Minister of Finance and not the Prime Minister who introduced this legislation. It is, it seems to me, another example of the indifference of the government in this matter. This, after all, was the final act of confederation. It was the kind of degrading act that I cannot imagine any of the Prime Minister's predecessors performing. Even if he had wanted the minister to make the speech, as is often done in this house, the resolution could have been put in the name of the Prime Minister. In a situation where there is already a good
5922	HOUSE OF
Grants to Newfoundland deal of feeling about this very point, it seems to me that there was a lack of constitutional propriety, a lack of a sense of the fitness of things in this matter.
There is one other thing which I want to say a very brief word about. The Minister of Finance regretted, as I think all Canadians regret, that the completion of confederation did not take place long before 1949. The minister said that if it had taken place before 1949 the people of Newfoundland would have made an even bigger contribution to the development of Canada than in fact they have made in those ten years since union. But I do not think we should just leave it at that, because notwithstanding the fact that the formal union did not take place until 1949 there had been a more intimate association between Newfoundland and Canada for a longer period than was perhaps the case between any two countries, even Canada and the United States, before union. The formal union was really a formal acceptance of what had almost become a fact before that.
The minister does not need to go further than the city and university with which he is so closely associated to recall that the greatest of our Canadian poets is himself a Newfoundlander. One could go on into almost any field. I reminded the house the other day that the president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority is a gentleman who happened to have been born in the settlement of Twillingate and who had part of his education in Bonavista. It is the same wherever you go in Canada. And this is not new, it has been true since the beginning of confederation in 1867 and even before it. It is statistically impossible to demonstrate this fact, but I would be very surprised indeed if there were not more people who had some of their origins, at any rate, in Newfoundland on the mainland of Canada than there are in Newfoundland, despite the growth of population there has been in the last ten years.
I come next to the second point which the Minister of Finance made this morning, which I wanted to take issue with, and that was the question of the duration of term 29. The minister attempted to show that this term was for a period of transition and that it was not meant to last indefinitely. Of course, the terms of union themselves demonstrate conclusively that that is not correct, because the very term before term 29, term 28, is precisely the term which deals with the period of transition. It is the term which provides for the transitional grants, and term 29 was to provide for something which was to take the place of the transitional grants if that were necessary. As has been said over and over again, there is no question


whatsoever that it was on term 29 that the negotiations almost failed, as the Leader of the Opposition pointed out this morning. It was the critical term, and it was the term on which Mr. Crosbie refused to sign the terms of agreement, because he felt that it was not an adequate safeguard. The hon. member for St. John's West, when he was in the parliament two before the last one, made statements in 1950 and 1951 about this which I have looked up, and he too had his doubts about the adequacy of this matter and was pressing at that time to have the royal commission appointed immediately and have this matter settled at an earlier date.
The Leader of the Opposition pointed out that there was absolutely no hint in term 29 of any time limit, no hint whatever. And there is no hint whatever of any time limit in the report of the royal commission. It is true, as the Minister of Finance has pointed out, that the royal commission was urged by counsel for the province of Newfoundland to recommend a periodic review, but the royal commission in its wisdom did not do that. I suggest that one of the reasons why they did not do that, which was set out in a letter by Professor B. S. Keirstead, of Toronto, published in the Globe and Mail of April 3, 1959, was that Mr. Ritchie, who at that time was counsel for the federal government, took exception to this suggestion and suggested that it was not within their purview.
But after all it is a rather fruitless thing for the Minister of Finance and myself to be discussing what was in the minds of the royal commission. What we have before us is not what was in their minds but what is on paper in their report. In the entire report there is not a word, or a hint, or a suggestion of any termination. I agree with the Leader of the Opposition and I agree with the premier of Newfoundland and I agree, to a very limited extent, with the Minister of Finance that a payment in perpetuity of $8 million is probably not the most suitable way of dealing with this problem, though I think that if the government had chosen to deal with it in that way they would have discharged the obligation under the terms of union to the letter, and I think that no valid criticism either on constitutional grounds or on grounds of good faith could have been directed against them if they had done that.
But I do think, as the premier of Newfoundland has said and as the Leader of the Opposition indicated earlier today, that an agreement between the federal and provincial governments to review this question on the basis and under the conditions provided in term 29 after a period of years would be better than the payment of $8 million in

perpetuity or for an indefinite period. I think the hon. member for Assiniboia put this point very well-that we do not legislate in perpetuity; we have a great many enactments with no time limit on them, but that does not mean that they cannot be changed by parliament within its sovereign power.
I would suggest, as the Leader of the Opposition suggested before me, that any unilateral change of this character is a repudiation of the spirit of the constitution and certainly of what the Newfoundlanders believed they were getting when they had this article written into the terms of union.
The Minister of Finance read article 29, and I am not going to read it in full again, but I should like to emphasize briefly once again what it was that this article was supposed to do. It was supposed to provide whatever difference of revenue was necessary to continue the public services at the level they had reached at the time of the inquiry as long as it was necessary to do that, without obliging the government of Newfoundland to impose taxes heavier than those in the maritime provinces. The minister says that the only express legal obligation was to appoint a royal commission and, of course, that is quite true. That is perfectly true, and that was recognized, as the minister said, by Mr. St. Laurent in the quotation which, again, I will not read because the minister has put it on record in Hansard.
But does anyone in this committee think for one moment that any of those distinguished Newfoundlanders who signed the terms of union would have signed if they had not had confidence in the good faith of Canadian public men, regardless of political party, to carry out the obvious intent of article 29? No one in his senses would have signed that document believing that if a royal commission was appointed the government of Canada had discharged its full obligation. No one in his senses would have signed it. Are we in this parliament going to say that because that is the only express legal obligation there is therefore no constitutional obligation? It seems to me that to ask that question is to answer it.
So little confidence did the hon. member for St. John's West and his colleague of those days, the late Mr. Higgins, have in this kind of protection that they campaigned, as I well know, in the year 1953, when I was elected to parliament, against the St. Laurent government, and the burden of their campaign was that the government of Canada should obligate itself to accept the report of the royal commission regardless of what it was. That was supported by their leader, Mr. Drew, in a speech at St. John's. In
Grants to Newfoundland other words, the position of the Conservative party under Mr. Drew in the year 1953 was that the royal commission's report should be accepted in advance regardless of what it contained.

Can the
hon. member give a citation in support of that?

I do not have them to hand but I will be glad to get them for the hon. gentleman and put them on record at the second reading stage of this bill.
I remember that situation very well, of course, because it was my first election. I was asked my own views on this subject and I repeated, though not literatim and verbatim, what Mr. St. Laurent had said. It was a big issue in Newfoundland at that time.
The Minister of Finance said there were two questions which arose concerning the recommendations of the royal commission. The first was that the commission gave no explanation of why it had departed from the year 1956-57 and taken the budget of Newfoundland for the year 1957-58 as the basis for its recommendation. The Leader of the Opposition dealt with that matter, I think. He made the point, but I should like to underline it a couple of times because the Minister of Finance did not seem to grasp it and because it does seem to be an important point. In 1956-57 the services were still being built up as they were in every previous year after 1949. The budget for 1957-58 was essentially to continue the services-because the word is "continue" not "maintain"-at the level they had reached at the end of the eight years. Of course, if a niggling, cheese-paring treasury board attitude were to be taken toward this matter of the final determination of confederation, perhaps some argument might be made about this, but it is an argument which I should be very surprised if hon. gentlemen opposite would carry very far.
The second question, the minister said, is what is meant by "thereafter". I am not going to argue that question because it seems to me to be very obvious that what is meant by "thereafter" is thereafter.
The minister has told us about the comprehensive study that has been launched into all aspects of fiscal policy. We on this side of the house have very grave reservations about that study. We have had a lot of experience of this kind of study going right back to 1936 and the Bank of Canada investigation into the three prairie provinces which was the foundation of the Rowell-Sirois commission. There was also the very

Grants to Newfoundland thorough study made in preparation for the dominion-provincial conference of 1945, and those studies have been going on continuously ever since. During that period a great many ideas have been contributed by many of the provinces themselves, as well as by the federal government. But the one thing to which everyone in Newfoundland objects most in the attitude of the present government toward this matter is its persistent attempt to assimilate this question of term 29 to federal-provincial relations generally. That seemed to be the position which was taken by the Prime Minister during the federal-provincial conference of November, 1957, when he said as reported at page 12 of that conference:
Now may I turn for a moment to the subject of fiscal relations In particular. As I view the situation, the first problem we have to consider is the need for some special recognition of the situation of the Atlantic provinces. There is, of course, a royal commission considering the particular problem of Newfoundland in accordance with the undertaking in the terms of union, so I shall not endeavour to express opinions upon Newfoundland's position pending receipt of the recommendations of the commision.
I believe that we all recognize, however, that the Atlantic provinces as a group are confronted with greater difficulties in public finance than the rest of the nation, if they are to maintain the sort of provincial and municipal services that Canadians generally expect. The taxable capacity of the Atlantic provinces, even in the best of times, is significantly lower than that of the other provinces.
This statement does contain-I am not going to put it in any other way than that- what certainly appeared to the premier of Newfoundland, and what certainly seems to me, to be an ambiguity. One can draw one of two conclusions from that statement, either that Newfoundland was expected to participate in this general treatment of the Atlantic provinces or, because of the royal commission, it was not. Mr. Smallwood was sufficiently concerned about that to devote a large part of his speech to it and the relevant parts are mainly on pages 99, 100 and 101. I do not want to take up the time of the committee by reading them but I would like to briefly summarize them.
What Mr. Smallwood said-and it was put very well by my friend the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo a little while ago-was that term 29 would provide Newfoundland with the necessary money to continue the existing level of services, and what these Atlantic provinces grants appeared to envisage was some improvement in their existing situation, and that surely Newfoundland was entitled to participate in that improvement, and that the fact that she was also having consideration given to the means of continuing the existing services should not exclude her from

participating with the other Atlantic provinces in the improvement. At page 101 the Prime Minister appeared to agree with that view. I will read the Prime Minister's words:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I will say no more at this time, but I would point out to the premier of Newfoundland that when I used the expression "the Atlantic provinces" I anticipated what his views would be in regard to the use of that expression.
I was present in the audience. I heard that statement and took from it what most other people took from it, that the Prime Minister agreed that these were two entirely separate things. But that has not been the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite since.
Last year when we were endeavouring to get these payments that were requested unanimously by the legislature of Newfoundland in a resolution moved by the premier and seconded by the leader of the opposition, the Minister of Finance used the Atlantic provinces grants as an excuse for delaying. This attitude is bitterly and universally resented in Newfoundland. The suggestion that because they are allowed to participate with the other Atlantic provinces-and certainly, as the hon. member for St. John's East pointed out this afternoon, their need is at least as great as any other Atlantic province and we think greater

is no reason why they should be denied their constitutional rights. That is our position.
There is just one other point I want to deal with before I come to the crux of this matter. The hon. member for St. John's East referred to the attitude taken in Newfoundland. He said something about narrow partisan views. I feel I should put on the record an article which appeared in the St. John's News of March 26, 1959, quoting a statement made by the leader of the Conservative opposition in the Newfoundland legislature. I do not suppose the hon. gentleman would accuse him of narrow partisan views on this question. The article is entitled, "Hollett: We Fail to Understand", and reads as follows:
Malcolm M. Hollett, leader of the opposition in the Newfoundland legislature and political leader of the Progressive Conservative party in this province, said he fails to understand the statement of the Prime Minister in relation to the provisions of term 29.
Mr. Hollett said in a statement to the Daily News "We scarcely know what to say. The royal commission recommended $8 million from the first of April, 1957, to be paid annually to the government of Newfoundland to enable it to continue public services at the levels and standards reached subsequent to the date of union. These are the words of the term itself."
"Rightly or wrongly," the opposition leader continued, "most of us thought that $8 million was too little. Even if $8 million were sufficient I fail to see how the federal government can accept the amount recommended by the royal commission

and then limit it to five years, which is contrary to the commission's recommendation in respect to time."

Would	the	hon.	member
permit a question?
Certainly.

Would	the	hon.	member
consider that to be a rude remark of a personal nature representing a personal attack such as I was referring to?

No. Mr. Chairman, I took down the hon. member's words and he said "narrow partisan views". He seemed to apply that to all the opposition to the government's attitute in the province of Newfoundland. I thought I should remind the hon. gentleman of this statement by Mr. Hollet.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member is trying to put words in my mouth that I did not use. I referred to those people in Newfoundland who made attacks of a personal nature on the person of the Prime Minister and the members of the government and said that their opinions reflected their own narrow political views.

I had not intended to mention this, but in that regard the hon. gentleman will remember that a delegation of students from Memorial University made a parade through the city of St. John's and they were led by a young man who was a prominent member of the young Progressive Conservative association. If that is what the hon. gentleman has reference to, that is all right with me.
Shame.

I had not intended to enter a discussion of this aspect of the matter at all. I merely wanted to correct the impression I thought was left by the hon. gentleman that there was something narrow or partisan about this opposition. I was in Newfoundland myself in the early days of April and I know perfectly well that it was extremely difficult to find anyone who did not share Mr. Hol-lett's views in greater or lesser degree. I now come to the crux of this whole situation.
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question before he moves on to another subject?
Certainly.

The hon. gentleman made a reference a little earlier to the fact that this resolution had been introduced by the Minister of Finance rather than the Prime Minister. Is it not a fact that through the years-and I think particularly of 1956 the
Grants to Newfoundland records of which I have before me-whenever financing arrangements were discussed and provision made by the house the resolution and indeed the bill itself was introduced by the minister of finance?

The Prime Minister has illustrated precisely my point. As the Prime Minister very well knows, those tax-sharing arrangements were financial arrangements made long subsequent to confederation, starting in 1941, dealing with the fiscal arrangements and tax-sharing between the provinces and the federal government. What I had earlier said, as the Prime Minister will find if he looks at my words, and what I repeat, is that it is this very attempt to degrade this measure into that field that is resented in Newfoundland. This measure deals with the constitution itself. This is the implementation of one of the terms of the British North America Act. This is the completion of confederation. It was for that reason and for that reason alone that I made the observation I did and I take it that my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition made similar observations. I feel very keenly about this matter. What is more, of course, the Prime Minister will recall that it was he and not the Minister of Finance who made the statement on March 25.
I might point out to the Prime Minister that I never took any exception to the Minister of Finance bringing in the Atlantic provinces grants legislation. I praised and supported them. I did not say the Prime Minister should have done it at all. That is one of the things that is quite within the normal departmental activities of the Minister of Finance. On the other hand I would not have blamed the Prime Minister if he had done it because I think it was about the only good thing this government has done in two years. However, he did not do it and I take no exception to that. But this is different. This measure is the completion of the constitutional framework of this country. I have no apology whatever to make for taking the position I have taken on this matter.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.
Would the hon. member permit a question-or he can carry on.
If the hon. member would like to ask a question I would be very happy if he would do so.
Does the hon. gentleman advocate payment of a definite, statutory grant in perpetuity?

No. That is precisely the point I was coming to. I do not advocate

Grants to Newfoundland that. I thought I had made that position clear, but I shall come to the very crux of this situation. The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo put the essence of this obligation very well, I thought more clearly than I had ever heard it put before and I have heard this matter discussed a good many times. It seems to me that the essence of this obligation is that Newfoundland should have the necessary revenue to continue the level of public services that was attained eight years after the union and to continue that without a level of taxation higher than the average in the maritime provinces. That is what the delegates thought they were getting. That is what they signed this for. They did not sign it to get a royal commission. They did not sign it to get $8 million for an indefinite period. They signed it to have that specific condition fulfilled. It might have been nothing or it might have been $20 million.
Indeed, the hon. member for St. John's East made a rather interesting point. He suggested that if the government of Newfoundland had increased its services instead of devoting some money to industrial development they could have had even better services by 1957. At least, I took that to be the import of what he said. That would have meant that a figure more than $8 million would have been recommended here.
But what I am saying is that a royal commission was the instrument by which this was to be determined, subject, of course, to the ordinary prudential considerations that have to be taken into account and subject, of course, to the final action of a sovereign parliament. There is a real problem, as the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance both well know and as I am sure most hon. members also know, with respect to our normal conception of parliamentary sovereignty and the conception of federalism. In a unitary state there is no problem. In a federal state there always is a problem and it was illustrated very well by the Leader of the Opposition this morning.
But subject to that limitation there was no question that this royal commission was the instrumentality to determine what was needed in this matter, and I say that what was needed in this matter and what will continue to be needed is the essence of the matter. That is what good faith demands that this parliament provide.
I do think if the government had accepted the recommendation no one, as I said earlier and I want to repeat it, could criticize the government on constitutional grounds. No one could accuse them of bad faith. They might be accused of niggardliness, and I am sure some have so accused them, but there could

I think perhaps considerable time of the committee might be saved if I made a short statement at this time. I propose to ask one of my colleagues to move an amendment to clause 16 when we come to that clause. As members of the committee will perhaps recall, this clause deals with the rate of interest. The amendment I propose is:
That paragraph (c) of clause 16 be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
(c) The interest rate on loans shall be 5 per cent per annum.
I observe, Mr. Chairman, that this announcement has apparently been received with universal acclaim throughout the committee.
I should like to explain, shortly, the reasons 

why the government has considered it desirable to make this change. We had proposed, and we still intend, that the farm credit provision shall be a self-sustaining one, that it will not be a scheme providing for a subsidized rate of interest. However, a large number of members of parliament from the Conservative party as well as some organizations made representations to the effect that the type of scheme which was provided for in the bill as it was introduced, and which was that the rate of interest charged should be the cost of money to the government, would cause the rate of interest to vary from year to year and would be unfair to those farmers who borrowed in years when the rate of interest happened to be relatively high as compared to those farmers who borrowed in years when the rate of interest happened to be low.
It was felt, therefore, it was more desirable to have what you might call an equalized interest rate; in other words, an interest rate which would be the same from year to year and which would be set over a period of years so that the amount of interest paid would be sufficient to pay the costs on the money which the government would put up for these loans. As a result we propose to make this amendment and to put into effect the 5 per cent interest rate which it is calculated will be sufficient to pay the cost of money to the government plus the ordinary carrying or administrative costs of the scheme. Mr. Chairman, we were pleased to hear the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) state that he would leave the rate of interest at 5 per cent. I must congratulate him and thank him for that, on behalf of the farmers. We realize he has understood the value of the claims we submitted at the resolution stage.
In fact, we had asked that the rate of interest be not higher than 5 per cent, and we had even recommended that it be made equal to the rate paid by the government on its loans. Besides, it is the same recommendation which was made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, as well as by all other farm organizations in general.
Having made other suggestions, we hope that on each item, the minister, having welcomed our suggestions, will introduce suitable amendments.
We suggested in the course of the debate that the bill be considered by the standing committee on agriculture and colonization, since this large scale bill involves far-reaching consequences; in fact, it should have

been referred to that standing committee so that it might have come back well prepared, well considered, polished and ready for efficient implementation.
The future of family farming is at stake. If we want to save the family farm, which is still the soundest unit of our national economy, it must be given the minimum of stimulus which its vitality and survival require.
In the province of Quebec, the number of farms is decreasing at the rate of 2,000 a year. Soon, with the farm laws being fostered by the Conservative government, it will not only be the number of abandoned lands that we will deplore, but actually the number of parishes. Our parish organizations, our school boards are deep in debt, and their burdens are becoming heavier and heavier, as a result of higher rates of interest.
What we need, Mr. Chairman, and what we have recommended many times, is the study of the very basis of the agricultural problem, which could be done if a federal-provincial commission were set up to consider particular farm conditions in each province.
Such a commission would have a huge and most useful task to accomplish, in the study of land use and conservation, readaptation of cultures and productions to their respective environments, and in the field of research, price products stabilization, marketing, etc.
We shall achieve those results when the Minister of Agriculture will have understood the problems of eastern farmers as well as those of western farmers.
According to the Gordon commission, it costs the Canadian taxpayers $1 billion a year to protect our industry in general. The agricultural class does not ask that much.
I do hope the Minister of Agriculture will fully understand the problems of our farmers, especially those of eastern Canada, so that, thanks to that new farm credit act, they may maintain themselves and prosper.
