Mr. Chairman, I must frankly admit that the minister's announcement was very pleasing to members of this group. I had intended to deal mainly with the interest rate and the inequalities of the interest rate. However, the minister has now scuttled my argument. Consequently I shall not have as much to say as had been my intention. Before proceeding I must say that we are pleased that the minister listened to
Proposed Long Term Credit to Farmers the arguments of the members of the opposition when the resolution was before the house. In my opinion he has taken a sensible course.
As one who appreciatss the value of the economic family farm in Canadian society, I am pleased indeed to see this measure come before the house. It is on that account that we support the measure in principle. It provides for supervised farm credit in reasonable amounts over a reasonable period of years and will make possible the maintenance, the improvement and the development of economic farm units in Canada. If the interest rate is maintained at not more than 5 per cent this measure could mean a new era in the use of agricultural credit in Canada.
We are in a somewhat better position with this bill than we were with the bill providing for crop insurance. There is definite and genuine experience upon which to base this legislation. That experience comes from the activities of the Veterans Land Act administration. I presume that this measure is based on that experience. I want to say once again-and I have no hesitation in saying this wherever I have the opportunity to speak on this subject-that this is to a great extent due to the dynamic and imaginative direction of the Veterans Land Act administration under Brigadier Rutherford supported by an extremely competent staff.
In that connection I want to bring to the attention of the committee some documents. I want to illustrate the imagination that has been used by the director of the Veterans Land Act administration and his officials in the preparation of materials that assists people to understand the results of the settlement of veterans under that act since the second world war. This shows a human interest in the problems of those we settle on the land and in their needs and requirements. It also shows an interest in making suggestions to improve the legislation.
I am not going to deal at length with them here, but I have here the Veterans Land Act administration quarterly comparative summary dealing with director's quarterly letter to all staff; self-analysis questionnaire for credit advisers; collection standing by districts and regions; number of special arrears by districts and regions; summary of work by districts; summary of work by regions and summary of work by fields. Then there is another pamphlet dealing with the organization, distribution and duties of staff, classifications and so on. Then there is another pamphlet pertaining to full-time farming settlement, part-time farming settlement,
5930	HOUSE OF
Proposed Long Term Credit to Farmers commercial fishing settlement, housing, civilian purchase contracts and various other matters. Then there is a very excellent book which deals with the summary of a survey of 5,000 V.L.A. farmers made between July, 1957 and September, 1958 for the purpose of assessing the progress and future credit requirements of farmers settled under the Veterans Land Act.
This demonstrates in an imaginative direction something we have not had before with respect to agricultural credit in this country. This is the sort of thing which lays a sound foundation for governments to pass legislation on, and I have no hesitation in paying a tribute to the excellent work being done by the Veterans Land Act administration. I would also say it is not only recognized by the members of this house and the veterans who have benefited from this legislation, but it is recognized by the Canadian Legion and other veterans' organizations. The Canadian Legion in its representations to the Senate committee on veterans affairs just recently urged the government to consider extending the same type of credit facilities which are provided to veterans under the Veterans Land Act to young Canadians who wish to commence farming in this country. It is an illustration of what has been done and can be done under this legislation for young Canadians who wish to commence farming.
On page 3 of this summary there is a table dealing with net worth, and it says:
The average net worth of the settlers, including the conditional grant of $2,320 as if earned at time of settlement, $5,376. The average net worth at time of survey, an average of 8.9 years after settlement, $13,487.
That is a clear, concrete illustration of the success which has been obtained under this legislation.
I want to make reference too to a paragraph on page 6, and I am putting this on the record because I think it is important that as many people as possible in Canada know what is being done under the Veterans Land Act administration, and know what can be done under this legislation now before the house, if it is used constructively and with the assistance of the Veterans Land Act officials. It says:
In this survey, we see 5,000 comparatively young farmers in all parts of Canada sitting down with their resident credit advisers and planning their future farm organization and production progams on the basis of at least some probability that ample supervised credit will be made available to them in order to carry out their plans. These men can see the possibility of increasing their net property and labour income by an average of about 60 per cent-which this survey has indicated to be possible and practicable-and of earning 30 per cent annually on the extra capital necessarily borrowed, or 24 per cent capital income after allowing $10 per day for the 40 days additional labour required. 

They are at the same time, and without even deliberately planning to do so, adjusting their future production in a way that, if made more general, would eventually largely eliminate surpluses of have-to-sell products such as wheat, and better ensure the required supply of high-protein refrigerator foods such as beef-for which there is an ever-increasing demand and which, on a calorie basis, take up to five times more land to produce an equivalent human ration. One can only speculate what would happen during the next ten years if even 50 per cent of the more progressive Canadian farmers with inadequate units did the same thing-which they undoubtedly would if given the opportunity.
I have no hesitation in saying that we are very glad they are going to be given the opportunity of this legislation.
The ultimate result would be fewer farms, but many more farms that could be classified as sound, economic, family sized units. Units in this class are able to make full and advantageous use of available labour and of the minimum equipment necessary to the production of a standard, readily marketable product on a production-line basis and at the lowest possible cost. There would seem to be little doubt that such units, given similar soil, climate and market conditions, could compete successfully over a long period with almost any corporate or integrated farm set-up.
That is very necessary for the success of the economic family farm.
If, through the use of adequate credit, Canadian agriculture could voluntarily reorganize itself over a period of years into economically sized family units, a considerably lower production cost and a higher quality product would ensure a fair profit at a lower selling price which would give Canadian farmers a safer corner on the home market now being threatened by the United States and New Zealand and put them in a much better position to compete in markets abroad.
To achieve this result through the medium of a controlled credit program would necessitate very careful credit administration in line with a consistent and long term policy, and much would depend on how well such a policy was accepted by farmers and farm organizations.
If V.L.A. farmers are at all typical of Canadian farmers generally, and we think they are, it would appear from the response to this survey that the great majority would welcome a credit program designed to encourage the voluntary reorganization of Canadian farms into economic family sized production units which would be more in line with present day capital and income requirements, and that they would be only too ready to co-operate fully in any long term program designed to assist with such voluntary reorganization. There would seem to be much to be gained and nothing to lose from such a program. Sound economic family sized units probably represent the most secure long term investment available which carries with it capital increment possibilities. The opposite could be said, however, of sub-marginal and inadequate farm units, since production costs on such units very often leave little or nothing in the way of profit with which to repay a capital debt.
I put that on the record because I think it is a very sound, but brief, analysis of the situation.
As I say, we were very pleased to hear the minister's announcement. Why should we

be doing this in view of the value of the economic family farm to Canadian society? It maintains many of the values in rural life which are very necessary if we are going to keep a healthy, democratic society in this country. We subsidize gold mines, we subsidize railways, we subsidize shipping companies, and we subsidize other industries. If we can subsidize this too I am sure that whatever slight subsidization results from maintaining the interest at 5 per cent will not only be supported by all members of this house but by farm organizations across Canada and the people of Canada generally. I have a number of constituents in my riding who welcome this legislation and who are in the very circumstances that this legislation is advanced to meet.
In conclusion, I have had my whole argument scuppered, and I wish the minister had let me know beforehand. I expected to spend about an hour on the deficiences of the bill, and it would have saved me some time. But we are pleased to hear this announcement and we accept it with pleasure. I might say we have a few suggestions to make and it is likely we will have an amendment; but our major criticism of the bill is met by the minister's announcement prior to the commencement of this debate.

As I was saying, Mr. Chairman, the "ventes a remere" system exists in the province of Quebec, and again I refer the minister to section 1546 and the following sections of the Quebec civil code. In a "vente a remere", the borrower, as a means of providing adequate security, sells his chattels to the lender. It doesn't matter what they are; they may be actual chattels or real property. Whichever they are, the maximum term allowed for a loan under the "ventes a remere" system is ten years. During that ten-year period, the vendor "a remere", who is in fact the borrower, may buy back the property he has given as security. That explains why the phrase "droit de remere" is known in English as "option of repurchase", or "right of redemption". The vendor has a right to buy back what he has sold, but this right must be exercised within ten years.
In the case of real estate, if the borrower or vendor "a remere" has repaid 75 per cent of the loan, he can require his lender, that is, the purchaser a remere, to grant him a mortgage.
If chattels are involved, whether they be livestock or farm equipment, the right to repurchase is retained for a maximum of 10 years. In such a case, the borrower cannot ask for a mortgage, because in the province of Quebec, as the minister no doubt knows- or perhaps his Quebec colleagues in the cabinet have told him-there can be no mortgages on livestock or chattels.
The minister will therefore realize the problems that may be raised in Quebec by this bill, particularly in the drawing up of contracts.

He said:	Mr. Speaker, His Excellency the
Governor General having been made acquainted with the purpose of this bill has given consent, so far as Her Majesty's property rights are affected, that the house may do therein as they think fit.
The object of this bill is to make a purely technical amendment to the Public Lands Grants Act. The amendment has to do with the transfer of the right of management of public lands from the federal government to

a provincial government or some other government of Her Majesty. The transfer of the right of management or administration is technically different from the sale of the land. When lands are sold there is a change in title. However, all public lands are vested in the crown, which is one and indivisible. The transfer of lands between one government of the crown and another does not involve a change in title. Transfers between governments of Her Majesty merely pass from one government to another the right to control the disposition of lands.
I might point out that the transfer of a publicly owned lot of land from the government of Canada to, for example, the government of the United Kingdom, does not in any way affect sovereignty. The transferred to remain within the jurisdiction of Canada as much as if a private individual had sold it to the government of the United Kingdom.
I should perhaps further point out that this bill has nothing to do with the transfer of lands to any government outside of the Commonwealth. It deals only with transfers from the government of Canada to provincial governments or other governments of Her Majesty.
Now, because an ordinary sale to a private individual is technically different from the transfer of administration to another government of the crown, the method of transfer is different. In an ordinary sale letters patent are issued transferring the title to the purchaser, letters patent being the form of deed used in conveyances by the crown. But because there is no transfer of title when administration is passed to another government of the crown the courts have long held that letters patent or a deed should not be used. The proper method according to the courts is for the transferring government merely to pass an order in council transferring the right of administration and control. This is the method which has been used by the government of Canada for many years.
The present section 4 (a) of the Public Lands Grants Act authorizes the sale of lands, but does not authorize the government of Canada to transfer the administration of public lands to another government of the crown. Nevertheless, such transfers were made as it was not thought that statutory authority was necessary. However, in a recent case in the Supreme Court of Canada, referred to in the explanatory notes in the bill, some of the judges said that transfers to the provinces by order in council are not valid unless the governor in council has the express authority of parliament to make such a transfer. It is to remove any doubt as to

speechtext:
Clause 9 provides for an advisory committee. It reads as follows:
9. (1) The Minister shall appoint an Advisory Committee consisting of a Chairman and at least six but not more than nine other members, the majority of whom shall be farmers or representatives of farm organizations.
(2)	The Advisory Committee appointed under subsection (1) shall advise the Corporation with respect to such matters arising under this Act as are referred to it by the Minister or the Corporation.
(3)	The members of the Advisory Committee may be paid for their services such remuneration and expenses as are fixed by the Governor in Council.
We are pleased that there is to be an advisory committee and that the majority of the members will be farmers or representatives of farm organizations but we feel that the advice of this committee should not be available only when sought expressly at the direction of the minister or of the corporation but rather that the committee should, of its own right, be able to tender advice to the corporation and to the minister. What will happen, in effect, if the advisory com-mitee has not the right to tender advice on its own is that its advice will seldom be sought, that the committee will meet very
5940	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Proposed Long Term Credit to Farmers seldom, if ever, and that in time its advice, if sought at all, will be requested with regard to some particular matter referred to it by the Minister of Agriculture. I think that is far too narrow a scope. I think it restricts unduly the function of such an advisory committee and will probably mean that the committee will be entirely useless. We have had experience with advisory committees set up under acts. We know that sometimes they are seldom called together and that their advice is sought not on important policy or controversial matters but with regard to details of questions which are not as important as questions involving major policy.
We had a discussion on this point in connection with the Agricultural Prices Stabilization Act and finally there was a provision made, if I recall it correctly, that the advisory committee should meet twice a year. However, there is no provision in this bill for regular meetings of the advisory committee. Unless something is done to meet this point the committee will have its hands tied and be unable to do its job of giving advice to the minister and to the corporation on what it feels are important policy matters. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Timiskaming:
That paragraph 2 of clause 9 be amended by deleting there from all of the words after the word "corporation" in line 19, and substituting therefore the following words: "and the minister on matters of policy within the term of this act."
Paragraph 2 would then read as follows:
The advisory committee appointed under subsection (1) shall advise the corporation and the minister on matters of policy within the terms of this act.
This would allow a competent and energetic advisory committee composed of farmers and representatives of farm organizations to give advice to the corporation and to the minister on matters of policy within the terms of the act. We have used the word "policy" to make it clear that we would not ask the advisory committee to pass on particular applications, but to look into the details of the operation of the board.
We have heard a great deal of strong criticism in this house of the Canadian farm loan board in recent years. I am certain that if there had been a strong and lively committee that had the right to tender advice to the board its administration would have been much better than it in fact has been.
We are hopeful that this new legislation will work in the long term interests of agricultural producers. We say again that we are pleased with the announcement that there shall be a fixed rate of interest. That will prevent an increase in the interest rate to more than 5 per cent as long as that provision

is in the bill. If the minister cannot accept this amendment we would have no objection to his accepting the spirit of it and wording it somewhat differently.
The idea behind the amendment is that the advisory committee should feel free to advise the corporation and the minister on main policies coming within the scope of the legislation.

Furthermore I do not believe that the amendment means too much, because, as the minister rightly explained, it is not simply because a farmer has suffered damages due to natural causes that he has lost all his power to borrow. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REPEAL OF THE CANADIAN FARM LOAN ACT

speechtext:
I should like to ask whether the minister has given any consideration to changing the method of making valuations of land. Most of the emphasis is put on land and therefore it is quite important that an over-all amount of money is not specified per acre for a particular area because of the variance from the real cost or real selling value of the land. I have had many complaints of valuations being made of only $25 a cleared acre and it has cost the farmers more than $25 just for the clearing of the land. In most cases it costs upwards of $50.
Therefore the farmers in my area at least feel that the valuations have not taken into consideration the real value of the land. They believe that this has been unfair and has tended to reduce the amount of money they can borrow on the land. I would think that there must be a fair relationship between the selling value of a farm and its appraised value, and quite often they have been

nowhere near the same amount. When the minister is setting up the new board I should like him to see to it that the board gives consideration to being more lenient and taking into account the actual sale value of the farm. I can give an example of a farm that was for sale at a price of $17,000. The valuation of the board was $10,000. The farm was sold a year later for $20,000. The person who applied for the loan had no opportunity to buy it at all because of the valuation. It meant that he was only going to get $7,000 to buy a farm that was going to cost him $17,000.

subtopic: REPEAL OF THE CANADIAN FARM LOAN ACT
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF LONG TERM MORTGAGE CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Once more, if the hon. member had studied the bill he would know this is provided for. Paragraph (a) of clause 19 (1) provides that the corporation may make regulations for:
(a)	establishing the basis and method of determining the appraised value of property for the purposes of this act, but the appraised value shall be based only on the value of the land for agricultural purposes and as far as possible on the productive value as shown by experience.
In other words, the appraisal will be made on the productive value of the farm for agricultural purposes. This clause was framed that way specifically so that land which is close to a city and has a value some years in the future, or perhaps immediately, for subdivision purposes or things along that line, will not be appraised on its value for building lots but on its value for producing agricultural products.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REPEAL OF THE CANADIAN FARM LOAN ACT
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF LONG TERM MORTGAGE CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: The minister should know that I have read that clause of the bill, and although I made one mistake earlier, in this particular case I think there is some difference of opinion between the purchase price and the productive value. The productive value depends entirely, in my opinion, on the use to which the farm is put. If a farm has not been in production for a number of years it will be very difficult for an outside appraiser to come in and say the farm is worth a certain amount. The selling price of that farm may be determined by other factors, some of which the minister has mentioned. I am quite pleased he is familiar with this problem. All I ask is that he give some instructions to some of the people who are doing this work because, in my particular area, the valuations by the Canadian farm loan board have been very low.
Clause agreed to.

speechtext:
I have some remarks to make with reference to this clause, as I did earlier this afternoon. I was very pleased that during the recess the minister considered the remarks I made. I am not fully satisfied with what he said shortly after eight o'clock on clause one of the bill. I am also pleased to know that the minister knows about the eastern townships. I may say that I come from that part of the country. I know there are some fine farms in that section, but that is not the situation all over Canada and it is certainly not the situation all over Quebec.
Having said that, I want to return to the subject I discussed earlier today. This clause 23 refers to supervised loans and to mortgages on farm lands and chattels. In my estimation the wording of the clause has the effect of joining the land and the chattels on the first mortgage. Now, as I said earlier, that is not possible in the province of Quebec under the civil code that is in force in that province. I know that earlier clauses of the bill provide that the corporation will have the power to prepare drafts of contracts to submit to the prospective borrower.
I repeat that I believe that in the province of Quebec, in order to make a loan on both farm land and on chattels it would be necessary to have two separate deeds, one deed for the land and another deed possibly for the cattle and farm equipment. The bill would be much clearer if we could separate these two things. I drew this amendment, and I put it forward now because I have another amendment to another section. I would move:
That section 23 be amended by deleting in line 3 thereof the words "on farm lands and chattels'* and by substituting therefor the following words: "on either farm lands or chattels or on both".
I feel that this amendment does not endanger at all the interpretation of the bill but it does give more opportunity, in my opinion, to farmers in Quebec to take part in the scheme for supervised loans. I hope the minister will agree with this proposed amendment to clarify that clause.

I do not believe there is any necessity for this, and actually the legal officers of the crown spent a great deal of time studying the best way in which to draft this clause in order to make it possible to make loans throughout Canada. So far as the province of Quebec is concerned, and this would apply in practically all the provinces, there would be two documents. There would be a mortgage on the land and there would be some document covering the chattels, which would be taken separately. As I say, the law officers of the crown, after a

speechtext:
The amendment I have
devised to clause 26 is in three parts. The first two parts are very much related to the amendment I presented to clause 23. I should like to say a few more words on paragraph (c) of clause 26. This paragraph reads as follows:
(c) the portion of the loan based on the appraised value of the land shall be repayable within a


period not exceeding thirty years and the remainder of the loan shall be repayable within a period not exceeding ten years;
Before I go any further I should like to ask the minister a question which I should like him to answer now. Is the ten years mentioned in the last part of the subparagraph in addition to the thirty years mentioned in the first part of the paragraph?

subtopic: REPEAL OF THE CANADIAN FARM LOAN ACT
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF LONG TERM MORTGAGE CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. You may have a case such as this. Suppose a man gets a loan for, say, $25,000. Of that amount $15,000 would be based on the appraised value of the land. The other $10,000 would be on the appraised value of the livestock, chattels and so forth. The amount on the appraised value of the livestock, and chattels would have to be paid off in 10 years and the amortization of the loan would be drawn with that idea in mind, namely the payment of so much a year to amortize it in ten years, whereas the other part of the loan based on the land would be amortized over 30 years.

subtopic: REPEAL OF THE CANADIAN FARM LOAN ACT
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF LONG TERM MORTGAGE CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
As I understand it, the maximum period on the livestock and chattels is 10 years. It seems to me, as I said earlier, that the amount to be repaid in the first 10 years will be a little bit too much for the farmer to handle if he is obliged to repay that amount at the same time as he is repaying on the land; that is, for the first 10 years. It is with that idea in mind that I have prepared and now wish to move an amendment which reads as follows:
That section 26 be amended in the following manner:
(a)	By deleting in line 24 thereof the words "on farm lands and chattels of the borrower" and by substituting therefor the following words:
"on either farm lands or chattels of the borrower or on both";
(b)	By deleting in lines 30 and 31 thereof the words "of the farm lands and chattels" and by substituting therefor the following words:
"of either the farm lands or chattels or of both"; and
(c)	By deleting in line 37 thereof the semicolon and the word "and" and by adding the following:
"provided that the former portion may not be made repayable before the date on which the latter portion is to be completely reimbursed".
The effect of this proposed amendment, especially the last part of it, is that the borrower will have to reimburse a portion of the mortgage loan in the first part of the period of the loan and the rest of the money borrowed in the last part of the period of the loan.

subtopic: REPEAL OF THE CANADIAN FARM LOAN ACT

Mr. Chairman, I think that most of these matters could more appropriately be covered by regulations made under the act than by being written into the legislation. The main point which the hon.

member raised was that payments would be too high during the first ten years. The amortization which would be provided for on a package deal of this kind would be such that the amount paid in would pay off the portion of the loan which was on the livestock and chattels during the first ten years and during that period the amortization payments on the land would really be very small. Therefore the difficulty of which the hon. member is afraid or which he has envisaged will not arise, in my opinion.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have made very good progress today, thanks to the cooperation of the two opposition parties. Tomorrow the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has to leave in the afternoon, so we will commence with item No. 4 on today's order paper, an agreement between the
federal government and the government of New Brunswick concerning Indian reserves. Then we will take item No. 7, a similar agreement with Nova Scotia; then item No. 10, concerning the convention on the nationality of married women. Then we will take item No. 12, the international wheat agreement; item No. 13, second reading of the Newfoundland grants act; item No. 2, the Senate amendments to the Income Tax Act, on which I think concurrence will be moved. Then we will take item No. 9, the act to provide for the humane slaughter of food animals.
The intention for Wednesday is to take up estimates, commencing with the Department of Trade and Commerce. Then we will take those of mines and technical surveys, fisheries and post office. We have a tentative agreement between the parties to sit from 2.00 to 2.30 on Wednesday and so long thereafter as we continue estimates, and an extra hour from 7.00 to 8.00 in the evening. I would hope that we could start next Wednesday evening, so we will then sit the whole of Wednesday evening and also take the extra hour from 7.00 to 8.00 on Thursday, Friday, and also sit on Saturday evening if necessary.
On Thursday the item No. 3 on today's order paper, the Senate amendments to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act, will be taken; then item No. 8, concerning the Combines Investigation Act. Then we will take the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and of the Secretary of State. On Friday we will take the estimates of the Privy Council, the C.B.C., national revenue, legislation and health and welfare, and on Saturday the estimates of finance.
Which Saturday will that be?
